turns.en: Today I'm chatting with three of my AI researcher friends, from whom I learn a lot every time we talk, and who also happen to be at somewhat open-ish labs and companies, so you guys can actually say things on the record. I'm joined by Beren, who is the CTO of Zyra, which is developing open source models; John Schulman, who is the chief scientist at Thinking Machines, previously the co-founder of OpenAI, and led the RLHF work that led to ChatGPT; and Charlie O'Neill, who is head of model training at Base 10.
turns.zh: 今天我和三位 AI 研究员朋友聊天，每次交谈我都从他们身上学到很多。他们恰好都在相对开放的实验室和公司，所以你们可以公开讲一些东西。和我一起的是 Beren，他是 Zyra 的 CTO，公司在开发开源模型；John Schulman，Thinking Machines 的首席科学家，此前是 OpenAI 的联合创始人，主导了催生 ChatGPT 的 RLHF 工作；还有 Charlie O'Neill，Baseten 的模型训练负责人。

turns.en: The first question I have: if we're in 2036, it's been 10 years, and we don't have crazy billions of crazy superintelligences running around that radically transform the world, what is the most likely reason that doesn't end up being the case? Other than exogenous political shocks, or there's a war, or they ban AI or something — what is the most likely technical reason that 2036 isn't a crazy alien superintelligence world?
turns.zh: 我的第一个问题是：假如到了 2036 年，已经过去 10 年，我们并没有成千上万、疯狂运转、彻底改变世界的超级智能，那么最可能的原因是什么？排除外生的政治冲击，比如爆发战争、或者 AI 被禁之类，最可能的技术原因是什么，让 2036 年没有变成一个疯狂的异形超级智能世界？

turns.en: I mean, my reason would just be that there's been a classic thing, almost like Moravec's paradox, right? We think of the AI being like — if it can do this, it's going to be amazing, right? If it can solve these hard math problems, if it can win at chess, blah blah. And then it solves these things, and then it's like, not that impactful. Obviously it's somewhat impactful, but not everything. It's like if somehow that continues, and there's never the true spark of generalization that occurs, I think that could lead to the AI just being extremely good at kind of everything that people put into a benchmark, put into an environment, but there are still some persistent sim-to-real gaps that are somehow blocking everything.
turns.zh: 我的理由大概是，有一种经典现象，几乎像莫拉维克悖论，对吧？我们想象 AI 是这样的——如果它能做这件事，那就会很了不起，对吧？如果它能解这些难题、能赢国际象棋等等。然后它真的解决了这些事，结果却没那么大影响。显然它有一定影响，但不是一切。如果这种情况一直持续，始终没有出现真正的泛化火花，我觉得那可能导致 AI 只是在人们放进基准、放进环境里的所有事情上极其擅长，但仍然存在一些持续的“仿真到现实”的鸿沟，不知怎么地卡住了一切。

turns.en: I think this is kind of unlikely. I think we do actually see this kind of generalization even from RL in practice already. But if it is just ridiculously hard to generalize — meta-learning plus we don't solve continual learning, it's just super hard and impossible — yeah, this would be my default scenario in that case.
turns.zh: 我觉得这有点不太可能。我认为在实践中，我们确实已经看到强化学习也能带来这种泛化。但如果泛化就是难得离谱——元学习，加上我们没解决持续学习，就是超级难、不可能——那在这种情况下，这会是我的默认情景。

turns.en: Yeah, I agree with that. Humans have a lot of advantages over models now, and each time a new model comes out, it'll sort of catch up in some of these areas. But you end up getting bottlenecked by the places where the model is weaker, where it has worse judgment, or where the models can't check themselves well enough. So there's this cycle that keeps repeating, where a new model comes out and people are blown away and they're like, this is it, this is AGI. But then they use it a bit, and then it starts to feel dumb after a month or so. So that cycle just might keep going, and it's hard to predict how many times it's going to repeat. And right now you don't get explosive growth in capabilities, because you still get bottlenecked enough when you're trying to do research and engineering that even if the model can write way more code than a person, it doesn't make you 100 times more productive. But yeah, so maybe there are just more of these cycles than we would expect.
turns.zh: 是的，我同意。人类现在相对模型有很多优势，每次新模型出来，它会在其中一些方面追上来。但你最终会被模型较弱的环节卡住——它判断力更差的地方，或者模型没法足够好地自我检查的地方。所以有一个不断重复的循环：新模型出来，人们惊叹，说就是它了，这就是 AGI。但用一阵子之后，大约一个月后它就开始显得笨了。这个循环可能就一直持续，很难预测它会重复多少次。而现在你得不到能力的爆炸式增长，因为做研究和工程时你仍然会被卡得够呛——即使模型能写的代码比人多得多，也不会让你效率提高 100 倍。所以，也许只是这类循环比我们预期的更多。

turns.en: For me, it's a question of how far off the global optimum of a learner you could have on a chip is — like the Transformer plus RL, basically the current recipe. People imagine that once you have an agent which is better than all humans at AI research, even if it's like 0.1% better than all humans, then the fact that you can run hundreds of thousands if not millions of these in parallel, you can run them much faster, chips are going to speed up — that's going to outweigh every other bottleneck, and you're eventually just going to hit this very fast takeoff with recursive self-improvement.
turns.zh: 对我来说，问题在于芯片上能有的学习器的全局最优离我们有多远——也就是 Transformer 加强化学习，基本上就是当前的配方。人们想象，一旦你有一个在 AI 研究上比所有人类都强的智能体，哪怕只强 0.1%，那么你能并行运行几十万甚至上百万个，能跑得快得多，芯片还会加速——这会压过其他所有瓶颈，最终你就会迎来递归自我改进带来的极快起飞。

turns.en: I could imagine that if we continue along the trajectory we're currently on with that paradigm — where it's basically just self-attention, RL, scaling up RL environments — I guess if you think about what happened with Moore's law, right? We had this very nice straight line, and that held for a really, really long time, but there were so many discrete discontinuities and innovations that had to happen to keep that scaling law going. And the same thing has kind of happened with LMs: we had this pre-training scaling law, and then that was kind of hitting diminishing returns, and then we came up with RL and solved that, and then we got this new diminishing-returns curve to hit, which made it keep looking like a straight line going up. So if it requires another one of those discontinuities to solve — I'm not sure that the current method of training LMs with these RL environments, even RSI-targeted RL environments, would be able to discover that discontinuity. And if not, we're probably going to hit this asymptotic curve where —
turns.zh: 我可以想象，如果我们沿着当前这个范式的轨迹继续走——基本上就是自注意力、强化学习、扩大强化学习环境——想想摩尔定律发生了什么，对吧？我们有过一条非常漂亮的直线，它维持了非常非常久，但为了维持那个缩放定律，必须发生许多离散的不连续性和创新。语言模型也发生了类似的事：我们有过预训练的缩放定律，然后它开始出现收益递减，接着我们提出强化学习解决了它，然后又得到一条新的收益递减曲线要突破，这让它看起来一直像一条上升的直线。所以，如果解决它需要又一次那样的不连续性——我不确定当前用这些强化学习环境训练语言模型的方法，即便是针对递归自我改进的强化学习环境，能否发现那个不连续性。如果不能，我们可能就会撞上这条渐近曲线，然后——

turns.en: Sorry, but do you think the discontinuity will be harder than anything that's come since 2012?
turns.zh: 抱歉打断一下，你觉得这个不连续性会比 2012 年以来出现的任何东西都更难吗？

turns.en: If we had the answer to that, we'd kind of have the ability to implement it. But maybe we should distinguish between a discontinuity which adds to the current paradigm — again, it's cumulative — and something beyond RL that we have to discover. And maybe they're capable of connecting the dots in that straight line.
turns.zh: 如果我们知道答案，我们大概就有能力实现它了。但也许我们应该区分两种不连续性：一种是给当前范式做加法的——同样是累积的——另一种是我们必须发现的、超越强化学习的东西。也许它们有能力在那条直线上把点连起来。

turns.en: Or, again, how far off the global optimum are we? Do we have to go back and throw out gradient descent and neural nets in general? And I don't think — if you continue to scale up the current paradigm, an LLM, no matter how many LMs you're running, is necessarily capable of discovering that if it's too far away.
turns.zh: 或者，还是那个问题：我们离全局最优有多远？我们是否必须回头把梯度下降和神经网络整个扔掉？我不认为——如果你继续扩大当前范式，一个 LLM，无论你运行多少个语言模型，如果那个东西太远，它未必有能力发现它。

turns.en: Yeah. The only hope really is if deep learning just can't get us to an AI which can at least dominate human research and human development, including the human ability to come up with new paradigms and so forth. Or, I don't know, maybe humans would also never have discovered the next learning architecture. But to the extent humans could have discovered it eventually — it just seems like, I don't know, if you just look at the progress that's happened from 2012 till now and you just continued that on.
turns.zh: 是的。唯一的希望其实在于：深度学习就是没法把我们带到一个至少能主导人类研究和人类发展的 AI，包括人类提出新范式等等的能力。或者，我不知道，也许人类也永远不会发现下一个学习架构。但就人类最终有可能发现它而言——只是看起来，我不知道，如果你看看 2012 年至今的进展，然后就这么继续下去。

turns.en: I mean, I know it's been powered by huge amounts of compute scaling and so forth, but it would be weird if it just didn't get to the point where it could dominate humans, at least in R&D, especially over the next few years. Ryan Greenblatt was on the podcast recently and he made this point that you could imagine as AI get more and more capable and are capable of making progress on simulations which incentivize getting better at not only AI R&D, but generally at science. So this is a thing that all the labs are targeting, many startups are targeting. Another intuition pump is if you look at the ELO score of chess bots since the 80s, there's just a very linear increase in ELO over time, but there's this huge discontinuity as they cross the human range of human experts. Human experts always win against AIs, then human experts never win against AIs as this linear increase happens. You could think I agree with your point that so far AI capabilities have not been that big of a deal in terms of their end economic impact in the world. But that is because they're slowly rising in ELO relative to humans.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，我知道它是由大量算力规模扩张等驱动的，但如果它没有达到至少能在研发领域主导人类的地步，那就很奇怪了，尤其是在未来几年。Ryan Greenblatt 最近上了播客，他提出了一个观点：你可以想象，随着 AI 能力越来越强，并且能够在模拟中取得进展，这会激励不仅提升 AI 研发能力，还能普遍提升科学能力。所以这是所有实验室都在瞄准的目标，许多初创公司也在瞄准。另一个直觉泵是，如果你看自 80 年代以来国际象棋机器人的 ELO 分数，ELO 随时间呈非常线性的增长，但当它们跨越人类专家的范围时，会出现巨大的不连续性。人类专家总是能赢 AI，然后随着这种线性增长，人类专家再也赢不了 AI。你可能会想，我同意你的观点，到目前为止 AI 能力在最终经济影响方面还没有那么大的影响。但那是因为它们相对于人类的 ELO 在缓慢上升。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean I agree it would be very—I mean the only way for this to not happen is if, as you say, somehow ASI just before—basically because we're already pretty close in my opinion to where we'll start crossing the human ELO score, and so we'll need to ascent before that. And that's the only way, you know, in the scenario you pose where somehow we're sitting here in 2035 and everything is normal for this to happen. I think the only other way is if there's some dramatic regulation on AI. It's kind of what I see as the most likely way for this scenario to happen actually, rather than the technical thing.
turns.zh: 是的。我的意思是，我同意这将会非常——我的意思是，唯一不让这种情况发生的方式是，如你所说，不知何故 ASI 就在——基本上因为在我看来，我们已经非常接近开始跨越人类 ELO 分数的时刻，所以我们需要在那之前上升。这是唯一的方式，你知道，在你设想的场景中，我们坐在 2035 年，一切正常，这种情况才会发生。我想唯一的另一种方式是对 AI 进行某种戏剧性的监管。实际上，我认为这可能是这种情况发生的最可能方式，而不是技术上的原因。

turns.en: Yeah, I think there's different kinds of research. There's research where it's like the auto research style where the objective is already specified very cleanly and you're optimizing that objective. And I think everyone is picturing like if we continue along this path of making pre-training loss go down, making our environments, making water go up, that's going to lead to improvement. But maybe what Ryan is talking about is this much more open-ended type of science which is required for paradigm shifts where we can't specify the objective and the AIs are definitely not able to specify that objective either. Like we have to be really really careful about how we specify objectives for any of these things.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为有不同类型的研究。有一种是自动研究风格，目标已经非常清晰地指定，你正在优化那个目标。我想每个人都在想象，如果我们继续沿着这条路径，让预训练损失下降，让我们的环境，让水位上升，那将导致改进。但也许 Ryan 谈论的是这种更加开放式的科学，这是范式转变所必需的，我们无法指定目标，AI 也绝对无法指定那个目标。就像我们必须非常非常小心地为任何这些事情指定目标。

turns.en: And maybe your point is that the nature of the breakthroughs that have happened since 2012 is that we have found—like in 2012 people weren't saying—or I'm assuming, I don't know, you guys were there or at least John you were there, but I was—
turns.zh: 也许你的观点是，自 2012 年以来发生的突破的本质是，我们发现——就像在 2012 年，人们并没有说——或者我假设，我不知道，你们当时在场，或者至少 John 你在场，但我——

turns.en: I was in primary school.
turns.zh: 我当时在小学。

turns.en: Actually, John, I'm curious for your wisdom of the ages, or wisdom of being in the trenches way back when, but presumably a big breakthrough was realizing that next token prediction is—you wouldn't have thought that nanoGPT speedrun is the thing to be optimizing for in 2014. But now that we have come to this new paradigm, you wouldn't think to do a speedrun on that and have you guys get really good at that. But maybe there's a next inner loop to optimize that the AIs wouldn't anticipate. And there's an outer loop of revenue or something that eventually should be strong. But it's a very slow outer loop.
turns.zh: 实际上，John，我很好奇你的岁月智慧，或者当年在战壕里的智慧，但大概一个重大突破是意识到下一个词预测是——你不会想到在 2014 年 nanoGPT 速度跑是要优化的东西。但现在我们已经进入了这个新范式，你不会想到对此进行速度跑并让你们变得非常擅长。但也许有一个下一个内循环需要优化，而 AI 不会预料到。还有一个收入的外循环或其他东西，最终应该会很强。但这是一个非常慢的外循环。

turns.en: Yeah. In fact, I remember in the early OpenAI days having the intuition that actually just minimizing log loss wasn't going to get you to intelligence because the important bits are accounting for such a small fraction of the loss that it was going to be overwhelmed by noise. So just training a language model on next token prediction just wasn't going to learn the interesting things you wanted to learn. And we needed to craft better objectives that would put more emphasis on the important things. And you can make all sorts of arguments for this and you could say, oh humans probably don't learn how to—we don't learn how to model everything in our environment. Most people can't create a photorealistic reproduction of some kind of scene they've looked at. So there must be—we must need a better objective. But then it turned out that it just worked anyway.
turns.zh: 是的。事实上，我记得在 OpenAI 早期，有一种直觉，即仅仅最小化对数损失并不能让你达到智能，因为重要的部分只占损失的一小部分，会被噪声淹没。所以仅仅在下一个词预测上训练语言模型，不会学到你想学到的有趣东西。我们需要设计更好的目标，更强调重要的东西。你可以为此提出各种论据，你可以说，哦，人类可能不会学习如何——我们不会学习如何建模环境中的一切。大多数人无法对他们看过的某个场景进行照片级逼真的再现。所以一定有——我们一定需要更好的目标。但后来发现它还是奏效了。

turns.en: And as you were pointing out, the inner loop even in current AI research of like post-training benchmarks or whatever doesn't necessarily translate into what users like.
turns.zh: 正如你指出的，即使在当前 AI 研究中，后训练基准测试之类的内循环也不一定转化为用户喜欢的东西。

turns.en: Oh yeah. I mean the whole field relies a lot on generalization and it's very hard to predict when you're going to get generalization or when you're going to get some kind of out of distribution generalization. So we know that if you train on the task you care about you're going to do better.
turns.zh: 哦是的。我的意思是，整个领域非常依赖泛化，很难预测你什么时候会得到泛化，或者什么时候会得到某种分布外泛化。所以我们知道，如果你在你关心的任务上训练，你会做得更好。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: But the most important advances are often the types of generalization that we have no right to expect. So for example from just pre-training on this very naive next token prediction objective to various tasks of interest where some require understanding of the input in some deep way or learning some skill from pre-training that's very rare and not very heavily represented. And then also generalization from these verifiable tasks to less verifiable ones. This is also a type of generalization that—
turns.zh: 但最重要的进步往往是那种我们本无权期待的泛化。例如，仅仅在这个非常朴素的下一个词预测目标上进行预训练，然后应用到各种感兴趣的任务上，其中一些任务需要以某种深刻的方式理解输入，或者从预训练中学习某种非常罕见且代表性不强的技能。然后还有从这些可验证任务到不太可验证任务的泛化。这也是一种泛化——

turns.en: There's no reason a priori to expect it.
turns.zh: 先验上没有理由期待它。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。

turns.en: So this is an interesting question because one intuition pump that you could have for why you would see some sort of singularity very rapidly without even scaling up the inputs to AI progress that are not just AI labor is that before every single experiment you run that's like a seven figure experiment you spend an equivalent amount of compute on AI labor and so you just have automated versions of you guys spending a century thinking about what is the optimal experiment to run, doing small scale ablations, developing literally a century's worth of theory. So going back even before deep learning, before you decide what experiment to run, doing extremely optimal setting up of the experiment. Then you do a century of thinking after the experiment is over where you're analyzing what happened and what the next experiment to run is.
turns.zh: 所以这是一个有趣的问题，因为一个直觉泵是，为什么你会看到某种奇点迅速出现，甚至不需要扩大 AI 进展的输入（不仅仅是 AI 劳动力），那就是在你运行每一个七位数实验之前，你在 AI 劳动力上花费同等数量的算力，所以你就有你们这些人的自动化版本，花一个世纪思考什么是最优实验，进行小规模消融，发展 literally 一个世纪的理论。所以甚至在深度学习之前，在你决定运行什么实验之前，进行极其优化的实验设置。然后实验结束后，你花一个世纪思考，分析发生了什么以及下一个实验是什么。

turns.en: Yeah. Well, I think if you think hard enough, you probably could have expected some of these things beforehand. Like there is probably some very clever way to do a small scale experiment that'll let you build the theory that then will generalize to the large scale experiments.
turns.zh: 是的。嗯，我认为如果你思考得足够深入，你大概可以事先预料到一些事情。就像可能有某种非常聪明的方法来做小规模实验，让你建立理论，然后推广到大规模实验。

turns.en: So I would expect that we're nowhere near the ceiling of how well you can do research. And I would imagine a future where AI is doing a lot of analysis and theory building, spending a comparable amount of compute to the amount that you're spending on the experiments themselves, doing various kinds of analysis and building a theory around what we've seen so far.
turns.zh: 所以我认为，我们在研究上能达到的水平还远未触及天花板。我可以想象这样一个未来：AI 进行大量的分析和理论构建，花费与实验本身相当的算力，进行各种分析，并围绕我们目前所见构建理论。

turns.en: I think there's really concrete examples of this when the objective is well specified. So again, all thinking can do is update your posterior based on the bits that you've gotten since you formed your prior. You can't gain any new bits from just thinking.
turns.zh: 我认为当目标明确时，有非常具体的例子。所以，思考所能做的只是根据你形成先验后获得的比特来更新你的后验。仅仅思考并不能获得任何新的比特。

turns.en: But when the objective is well specified and there is this data sitting around, I imagine there will be this big speed up in the current paradigm we're in. And a good example of this is if you got an AI to think about the Kaplan scaling laws, an AI at this point would have noticed that they've just taken these intermediate checkpoints and didn't account for the annealing, and so this is wrong, and that would have caught that years earlier. We would have made progress—would have cut off a year or two of progress just from that observation from an AI.
turns.zh: 但当目标明确且周围有这些数据时，我想在当前范式下会有很大的加速。一个很好的例子是，如果你让 AI 思考 Kaplan 缩放定律，此时的 AI 会注意到他们只是取了这些中间检查点，而没有考虑退火，所以这是错误的，那会早几年发现。我们本可以取得进展——仅从 AI 的那个观察就能节省一两年的进展。

turns.en: And again, once the objective is well specified, which is like lower pre-training loss or whatever, there's many many good examples where if you just thought about it a bit more you would have been able to cut down significantly on things that you've done. So like mu and how learning rate scales with model size and realizing that model width is important in that as well. I feel like you can really back out a lot of these things and cut off a lot of low hanging fruit. So I would imagine a 10 times speed up if our thing is just to maximize the objective we're currently on.
turns.zh: 再说一次，一旦目标明确，比如降低预训练损失之类的，有很多很多好例子，如果你再多思考一下，就能大幅减少你已经做的事情。比如 mu 以及学习率如何随模型规模缩放，并意识到模型宽度在其中也很重要。我觉得你真的可以推导出很多这些东西，并摘掉很多低垂的果实。所以，如果我们的目标只是最大化当前的目标，我想象会有 10 倍的加速。

turns.en: But I don't see how that generalizes at all to coming up with the right objective in the first place. Just thinking doesn't necessarily buy you the right objective in the first place.
turns.zh: 但我看不出这如何推广到首先提出正确的目标。仅仅思考并不一定能让你首先获得正确的目标。

turns.en: Yeah, I think this is really the key question to any kind of very rapid RSIs from current AI: how well can AI generalize to learning their own objectives? Because to have any kind of self-propelling automated loop, you need the AI to propose objectives, optimize them, figure that out, propose a new objective, and have this not go off the rails at any point for a long long time. Coming back to MVX products, there might be a case of MX products where we think this kind of autonomy and being self-encapsulated so we can think of what we should do ourselves and then go do it and have this loop is super easy because we always do this. And obviously evolution needs to create creatures that can survive on by themselves for long periods of time, and this just might be something that for some reason is really hard for the AI in the same way that locomotion stuff is really hard. Math is super easy despite being super hard for us.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这对当前 AI 的任何快速递归自我改进来说都是关键问题：AI 在多大程度上能泛化到学习自己的目标？因为要有任何自驱动的自动化循环，你需要 AI 提出目标、优化它们、弄清楚，提出新目标，并确保这在很长很长一段时间内任何时候都不偏离轨道。回到 MVX 产品，可能有 MX 产品的情况，我们认为这种自主性和自我封装，以便我们可以自己思考应该做什么然后去做，并拥有这个循环是超级容易的，因为我们总是这样做。显然，进化需要创造能够长时间独立生存的生物，而这可能对 AI 来说由于某种原因非常困难，就像运动 stuff 非常困难一样。数学超级容易，尽管对我们来说超级难。

turns.en: I don't know. Doesn't the time horizon increasing suggest that that's—
turns.zh: 我不知道。时间跨度的增加难道不表明那是——

turns.en: Yeah, exactly. I mean this is another possibility, but I agree there's no obvious evidence for this. In fact—
turns.zh: 是的，没错。我是说这是另一种可能性，但我同意没有明显的证据。事实上——

turns.en: The fact that you know agent is now super persistent and it's quite easy to do this is kind of evidence against this.
turns.zh: 你知道智能体现在超级持久，而且做这个相当容易，这有点是反对这一点的证据。

turns.en: But this would be potentially one of the reasons why we just don't get this immediate takeoff is if this is hard.
turns.zh: 但这可能是我们没有立即起飞的原因之一，如果这很难的话。

turns.en: If you look back from 2012 till now or maybe from when you started doing your research till now, what part of all the innovations that have happened since that time, including purely engineering ones, including purely conceptual ones, what seems like the thing that would be the last things humans would have to do before AI is totally automate AI R&D?
turns.zh: 如果你回顾从 2012 年到现在，或者从你开始做研究到现在，自那时以来发生的所有创新中，包括纯工程的、纯概念的，哪部分看起来是 AI 完全自动化 AI 研发之前人类最后要做的事情？

turns.en: Probably just iteratively asking the right questions. If you can get the AI to do any experiment, but you need to decide what experiments to do. And right now, I think AI are not very good at this compared to coding the experiments at all.
turns.zh: 可能只是迭代地提出正确的问题。如果你能让 AI 做任何实验，但你需要决定做什么实验。而现在，我认为 AI 在这方面与编码实验相比还不太擅长。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah, like whenever we talk about research, they proposed a bunch of miscellaneous things which are very very tiny steps.
turns.zh: 是的。是的，就像每当我们谈论研究时，他们提出一堆杂七杂八的东西，都是非常非常小的步骤。

turns.en: Or even going from DeepMind's approach of 'we're going to solve intelligence by learning to play games at a superhuman level'—that's going to be the approach—to one random researcher like Radford being like 'I'm going to try and just predict the next token off a very wide swath of data.'
turns.zh: 甚至从 DeepMind 的方法“我们将通过学会在超人水平上玩游戏来解决智能”——那将是方法——到像 Radford 这样的一个随机研究员说“我将尝试从非常广泛的数据中预测下一个词。”

turns.en: And then even once Radford had discovered that, it took a while before people decided to scale it up because we had to come up with the idea of scaling laws and the fact that you could very reliably predict these things.
turns.zh: 然后即使 Radford 发现了这一点，人们决定扩大规模也花了一段时间，因为我们必须提出缩放定律的想法，以及你可以非常可靠地预测这些事情。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. I would say that the last job for humans or the role for humans that'll last the longest is defining the objective and deciding what we actually want. So in that vein, something like deciding how the AI assistant should behave or what it means to be helpful or what's the objective when we're doing RLHF is one such thing, and then later defining constitutions and model specs is another one. And I think even if the AIs can do all the technical work, we'll have to still do a lot of that and decide what we actually want.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。我会说人类最后的工作或持续时间最长的角色是定义目标和决定我们真正想要什么。所以在这方面，比如决定 AI 助手应该如何表现，或者什么是有帮助的，或者我们在做基于人类反馈的强化学习（RLHF）时的目标是什么，就是其中之一，然后后来定义宪法和模型规格是另一个。我认为即使 AI 能完成所有技术工作，我们仍然必须做很多这方面的工作，并决定我们真正想要什么。

turns.en: Yeah, alignment is the final job.
turns.zh: 是的，对齐是最后的工作。

turns.en: Yeah, alignment is sort of the answer, but it's also—alignment itself can be kind of decomposed into specification of the objective or figuring out what the right objective should be, and then actually achieving or optimizing the objective you've defined. And I think the first one is not going to go away anytime soon. And if I think about a post-training team and why you need a lot of people to be on the team, it's just because there are a lot of different areas where you have to figure out how the model should behave, and there's no way—it would be very hard to automate the whole thing just because someone has to think about how should the model behave in this area.
turns.zh: 是的，对齐算是答案，但也是——对齐本身可以分解为目标的 specification 或弄清楚正确的目标应该是什么，然后实际实现或优化你定义的目标。我认为第一个不会很快消失。如果我想到一个后训练团队以及为什么需要很多人在团队中，那是因为有很多不同的领域你需要弄清楚模型应该如何表现，而且没有办法——很难自动化整个过程，因为必须有人思考模型在这个领域应该如何表现。

turns.en: Jane Street started using Antithesis to test our software in early 2025 and they were so impressed by the product that they decided to invest in the company.
turns.zh: Jane Street 在 2025 年初开始使用 Antithesis 来测试我们的软件，他们对产品印象深刻，于是决定投资这家公司。

turns.en: I recently caught up with Ron Minsky who co-leads Jane Street's tech group to ask about how Antithesis actually plugs in.
turns.zh: 我最近采访了 Ron Minsky，他共同领导 Jane Street 的技术团队，我问他 Antithesis 实际上是如何接入的。

turns.en: The thing that I think is most impressive about Antithesis is we started using it in a team that was building high assurance software and being really careful and nonetheless it was able to shake out bugs that were otherwise going to be really hard to find. And that's important both because it helps make those systems more reliable, but also because it helps the teams that build it to just move faster.
turns.zh: 我认为 Antithesis 最令人印象深刻的一点是，我们开始在一个构建高保障软件的团队中使用它，团队非常谨慎，但它仍然能够找出那些原本很难发现的 bug。这很重要，既因为它有助于使这些系统更可靠，也因为它帮助构建这些系统的团队更快地推进。

turns.en: This matters more and more as code production is increasingly automated.
turns.zh: 随着代码生产越来越自动化，这一点变得越来越重要。

turns.en: I think in general as we've been using agents more and more, the key problem that you run into is the verification bottleneck. Just the time it takes from people to look at code and figure out is that actually something you want to accept in your production software. And tools that make testing better are just incredibly helpful there. You just ease the verification bottleneck and make it possible for you to get more stuff done and move faster because you can have more confidence that the code generated by the agent is actually not introducing new problems.
turns.zh: 我认为总的来说，随着我们越来越多地使用智能体，你遇到的关键问题是验证瓶颈。就是人们需要花时间查看代码并弄清楚那是否真的是你想接受的生产软件。而让测试更好的工具在这方面非常有帮助。你只需缓解验证瓶颈，就能完成更多工作并更快推进，因为你可以更有信心地认为智能体生成的代码实际上没有引入新问题。

turns.en: To see how Antithesis fits into your development process, go to antithesis.com/bash.
turns.zh: 要了解 Antithesis 如何融入你的开发流程，请访问 antithesis.com/bash。

turns.en: What is the story for why there isn't huge consolidation in model providers? There's just so many things that point to centralization here. If we step back over the course of years is there something that is gonna prevent that?
turns.zh: 为什么模型提供商没有出现大规模整合？这里有很多因素都指向集中化。如果我们回顾过去几年的情况，有什么会阻止这种趋势吗？

turns.en: Yeah I think distillation is the main thing that fights against the centralizing force because basically anything that can be learned through RL can be distilled very easily because it's a small number of bits, it's something that you can learn from a small amount of data. So if you can get trajectories from the model that show a behavior you can easily distill it. So I think distillation is one of the things that fight centralization. There's also a possibility that there'll be company specific models that it'll be possible to learn from deployment and have a company continually improving its own model.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为蒸馏是抵抗集中化力量的主要因素，因为基本上任何可以通过强化学习学到的东西都可以很容易地被蒸馏，因为它只是少量比特，你可以从少量数据中学到。所以如果你能从模型中获得展示某种行为的轨迹，你就可以轻松地蒸馏它。所以我认为蒸馏是抵抗集中化的因素之一。还有一种可能性是会出现公司特定的模型，可以从部署中学习，并让公司不断改进自己的模型。

turns.en: Such a system could be provided by the current oligopoly of model providers or some other currently smaller company, but I think that'll change the game a bit.
turns.zh: 这样的系统可以由当前的模型提供商寡头或一些目前较小的公司提供，但我认为这会稍微改变游戏规则。

turns.en: Yeah and I also want to point out that continual learning doesn't stop distillation, right? Like even if your model is improving every day, people could be distilling it every day. So the loops could just operate at the same pace.
turns.zh: 是的，我还想指出，持续学习并不能阻止蒸馏，对吧？就像即使你的模型每天都在改进，人们也可能每天都在蒸馏它。所以循环可以以相同的速度运行。

turns.en: Right? That makes sense. Okay, so copying model behavior, I guess you need to know yourself what the right distribution to prompt is in order to get the relevant model behavior.
turns.zh: 对吧？这说得通。好的，那么复制模型行为，我猜你需要自己知道正确的提示分布是什么，才能获得相关的模型行为。

turns.en: Oh yeah, for just distilling with supervised learning the prompt distribution is extremely important. So it's very non-trivial to distill a model even if you have full access to it and have the chain of thought and everything. Yeah it's non-trivial to distill all of the useful capabilities from it. Because you need to prompt the model with something and you need to prompt it with realistic prompts. You need to have a really wide distribution of realistic prompts. So yeah, one thing that's been coming out recently is some of the Chinese companies are probably using these router services which are designed to allow people in China to use the US frontier models which would otherwise be blocked in China. But there are all these router or proxy services that allow people in China to use these models mostly for coding and these router services are collecting and selling some of the data. So I think this is a very useful data set for distillation because it gives you the perfect prompt distribution.
turns.zh: 哦是的，对于用监督学习进行蒸馏来说，提示分布极其重要。所以即使你完全访问模型并拥有思维链等一切，蒸馏模型也是非常不简单的。是的，从中蒸馏所有有用的能力是不简单的。因为你需要用一些东西来提示模型，并且需要用现实的提示来提示它。你需要有一个非常广泛的现实提示分布。所以是的，最近出现的一件事是，一些中国公司可能正在使用这些路由服务，这些服务旨在让中国的人们使用原本在中国被封锁的美国前沿模型。但有所有这些路由或代理服务，允许中国的人们使用这些模型，主要用于编程，而这些路由服务正在收集和出售一些数据。所以我认为这是一个非常有用的蒸馏数据集，因为它为你提供了完美的提示分布。

turns.en: Yeah, I think this is one of those things where AI helps a lot here. Like if you actually look at the frontier pipelines of say the Chinese models that they actually put in their papers, it's a lot of humans or they get seed prompts from somewhere which is some combination of humans, this kind of data, and then they synthesize a vast coverage from those seed prompts using their existing models or other frontier models. And so you can automate an awful lot of this prompt distribution gathering and environment creation. It's just humans need to provide increasingly few amounts of bits. As the models get better.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这是 AI 在这方面帮助很大的一件事。就像如果你真的看看中国模型的前沿流程，他们在论文中实际提出的，很多是人类，或者他们从某个地方获得种子提示，这是人类、这类数据等的某种组合，然后他们使用现有模型或其他前沿模型从这些种子提示中合成大量覆盖。所以你可以自动化大量的提示分布收集和环境创建。只是随着模型变得更好，人类需要提供的比特越来越少。

turns.en: Right? But it seems you're still bottlenecked by having a service which has users or users are going through.
turns.zh: 对吧？但似乎你仍然受限于拥有一个拥有用户或用户正在使用的服务。

turns.en: Not necessarily. I mean, that's obviously very helpful, but theoretically you can just think about what users want or like...
turns.zh: 不一定。我的意思是，那显然非常有帮助，但理论上你可以只考虑用户想要什么，或者像……

turns.en: Like the whole point is that we don't... the user says make me an application like this. Oh that didn't... I actually want you to make this new feature but actually let's step back and do this other thing and capturing that whole trace is the... or to the extent you could have done that anyways then you just have like RSI any...
turns.zh: 就像整个重点是，我们不……用户说给我做一个这样的应用。哦那没有……我实际上想让你做这个新功能，但实际上让我们退一步做另一件事，捕捉整个轨迹是……或者如果你无论如何都能做到这一点，那么你就有了递归自我改进……

turns.en: Yeah, I mean ultimately if you have this fully automated loop that is basically RSI right? Like the AI is deciding the data, it's deciding the training, that is the loop. But yeah, it depends how much human information you need. Like at some point if you're just like I want traces that look like this, you prompt that to the model, the model will be able to come up with a pretty good approximation.
turns.zh: 是的，我的意思是最终如果你有这个完全自动化的循环，那基本上就是递归自我改进，对吧？就像 AI 决定数据，决定训练，那就是循环。但是的，这取决于你需要多少人类信息。就像在某个时候，如果你只是说“我想要看起来像这样的轨迹”，你向模型提示，模型就能给出一个相当好的近似。

turns.en: But what if you want to do like make me a really good politician and anticipate de novo like how would discussion in the Senate halls go or something. I just feel like there's going to be a lot of things.
turns.zh: 但如果你想做的是，比如让我成为一个真正优秀的政治家，并从头预测参议院大厅里的讨论会如何进行之类的。我只是觉得会有很多事情。

turns.en: Ironically, this is actually I think easier for the distillers than the frontier labs, right? Because the distillers just like I want a good politician, they go to the frontier model. The frontier model already knows how to be a good politician. So it just generates those traces. Whereas if you actually want to build the first model that does this, you have to actually somehow get data on what politicians do every day and build that. So it's actually much easier to say I want something like this and then get the AI to produce a billion variations to actually create the thing to begin with.
turns.zh: 讽刺的是，我认为这对蒸馏者来说实际上比前沿实验室更容易，对吧？因为蒸馏者只是说“我想要一个优秀的政治家”，他们去找前沿模型。前沿模型已经知道如何成为一个优秀的政治家。所以它只是生成那些轨迹。而如果你真的想构建第一个做到这一点的模型，你必须以某种方式获取政治家每天做什么的数据并构建它。所以说“我想要这样的东西”，然后让 AI 产生十亿个变体来实际创造这个东西，实际上要容易得多。

turns.en: I think you can actually make a really concrete prediction based off this observation that the Chinese labs have this router data.
turns.zh: 我认为你实际上可以基于中国实验室拥有这些路由数据的观察做出一个非常具体的预测。

turns.en: Like I think the thing that just stated this originally was I was saying isn't it weird how set 5 and opus 5 are like almost objectively worse models than like GLM 5.3 Kim K3 even though they've had access to like not only distillation but logic distillation from like mythos and so the counter here was that like okay the prompt distribution really really matters. Like you need to see what users are doing so you can distill like kind of these behaviors and things in. I think the prediction from this is that the frontier labs don't necessarily have much of an advantage if at all in RL environments now because yes like user distribution matters for like general like behavior and so on but like the best measure of a capability is the very very hard RL environments you've made at the frontier and so if you have access to those RL environments as Anthropic and you have access to logic distillation and you've still made a worse model then maybe real world deployment matters more than the environment. That's really interesting. So but they had to incentivize those capabilities in the first place in Fable or the Frontier model.
turns.zh: 就像我觉得最初提出这一点的是我，我说：难道不奇怪吗？Set 5 和 Opus 5 几乎客观上是比 GLM 5.3、Kimi K3 更差的模型，尽管它们不仅能做蒸馏，还能从 Mythos 做逻辑蒸馏。所以这里的反驳是：好吧，提示分布真的非常非常重要。你需要看到用户在做什么，才能蒸馏出这些行为等等。我认为由此得出的预测是，前沿实验室现在在强化学习环境上不一定有多大优势，甚至可能没有优势，因为是的，用户分布对通用行为等很重要，但衡量能力的最佳标准是你在前沿构建的非常非常难的强化学习环境。所以如果你像 Anthropic 一样能访问那些强化学习环境，又能做逻辑蒸馏，却仍然做出了更差的模型，那么也许现实世界的部署比环境更重要。这真的很有趣。所以他们首先必须在 Fable 或前沿模型中激励那些能力。

turns.en: And so it's weird that they can't incentivize them again.
turns.zh: 所以奇怪的是他们不能再激励一次。

turns.en: Or with a smaller model or something.
turns.zh: 或者用更小的模型之类的。

turns.en: Maybe we're just in this weird uncanny valley where actually trying to copy that frontier model too much, the student-teacher gap or whatever it is, is just too large. And I think people made this point with Opus: the difference between Opus 4.6 and Opus 5 is that Opus 5 really feels like it's got this AI as a judge checking every possible thing it's done, and that's why it uses so many tokens. It tries to think about all these things but it doesn't necessarily have the big model smell of Fable to know when to stop doing that or when's the good path to go down or whatever.
turns.zh: 也许我们只是处在这个奇怪的恐怖谷中，实际上试图过多地复制那个前沿模型，学生-教师差距或其他什么，就是太大了。我认为人们用 Opus 提出了这一点：Opus 4.6 和 Opus 5 的区别在于，Opus 5 真的感觉它有一个 AI 作为裁判检查它所做的每一件可能的事情，这就是为什么它使用这么多 token。它试图思考所有这些东西，但它不一定有 Fable 的大模型嗅觉，知道什么时候停止这样做，或者什么时候是好的路径之类的。

turns.en: The reach exceeds the grasp.
turns.zh: 目标超出了能力。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: Yeah. I would offer a slightly different hypothesis. So I would say there are a couple of different axes for the environments you can create, and one of them is difficulty and the other is realism. It's comparatively easy to create a lot of difficult environments that involve doing a much more complicated task or doing something that requires a lot more cleverness. And you could say this is like the benchmaxing distribution because a lot of the most prominent benchmarks just involve doing some very hard puzzle-like task that's easy to verify. And then there's the realism axis where you want the model to be good in the realistic coding agent setting where there's multiple back and forth with the human and there's multiple objectives. And I'd say the labs who are crafting the model behavior for the first time need to push in both directions and to get good model behavior you need to really push on the realism axis and have rubrics or some kind of human feedback that's informing the reward function you use there. But I think when you try to do distillation naively, you end up just matching the teacher on the benchmaxing distribution. And if you don't have enough of the environments that really exercise the capabilities in these trickier realistic settings, then you're not going to get those into your student model. And I think maybe one thing that's happening is the big models generalize better from the tricky narrow tasks to these more realistic tasks. So if you have a really good realistic prompt distribution for distillation, you can match the big model really well. But if you only have this distribution of easily verifiable tasks, then you can match the big model on all the benchmarks but you do worse on this broader distribution. So that might even explain something about the smaller Anthropic models like Sonnet 5, though it's hard to predict exactly what they're doing to post-train those models. It could also be that they're always changing their post-training stack and they just got a few things wrong in some of these models. So they turned up something too high and created some quirks that people really don't like. So it's really easy to screw up post-training in some way that doesn't show up in benchmarks. I mean just one other very basic point is just like the frontier AI labs buy all their data from big data companies and the Chinese can also just buy the same data from data companies and they are exactly—there's a lot of people being annoyed about this—but if they have exactly the same data and they can buy that, they can also distill, it means it's quite easy to keep up really.
turns.zh: 是的。我想提出一个稍微不同的假设。我认为你可以创建的环境有几个不同的轴，一个是难度，另一个是现实性。相对容易创建大量困难的环境，这些环境涉及做更复杂的任务或需要更多聪明才智的事情。你可以说这就像是刷榜分布，因为许多最突出的基准测试只是涉及做一些非常难的、像谜题一样的任务，这些任务容易验证。然后是现实性轴，你希望模型在现实的编码智能体设置中表现良好，那里有与人类的多次来回交流，有多个目标。我认为第一次塑造模型行为的实验室需要在两个方向上推进，而要获得良好的模型行为，你需要真正在现实性轴上推进，并有评分标准或某种人类反馈来为你在那里使用的奖励函数提供信息。但我认为当你天真地尝试蒸馏时，你最终只是在刷榜分布上匹配教师模型。如果你没有足够的环境来真正锻炼这些更棘手的现实设置中的能力，那么你就不会把这些能力带入你的学生模型。我认为可能发生的一件事是，大模型从棘手的狭窄任务到这些更现实的任务的泛化能力更好。所以如果你有一个非常好的现实提示分布用于蒸馏，你可以很好地匹配大模型。但如果你只有这种容易验证的任务分布，那么你可以在所有基准测试上匹配大模型，但在这个更广泛的分布上表现更差。所以这甚至可以解释一些关于较小的 Anthropic 模型如 Sonnet 5 的事情，尽管很难准确预测他们在后训练那些模型时做了什么。也可能是他们总是在改变他们的后训练技术栈，他们只是在一些模型中弄错了几件事。所以他们把某个东西调得太高，创造了一些人们真的不喜欢的怪癖。所以很容易在后训练中搞砸，而这些问题不会在基准测试中显示出来。我的意思是，另一个非常基本的点是，前沿 AI 实验室从大数据公司购买所有数据，中国人也可以从数据公司购买同样的数据，他们完全——有很多人对此感到恼火——但如果他们有完全相同的数据，他们可以购买，他们也可以蒸馏，这意味着很容易跟上。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Okay. The other question I had is how the first models that are capable of automating AI R&D will actually be trained because there's a toy version which is this thing that Ryan was talking about which is you just have GPT8 try to build GPT3 size models that are really good at like inner loop type challenges of beating video games that require continual learning or just getting to a certain loss with the least amount of compute etc. But John, I think you had an interesting point that maybe that's not the way it actually will happen in practice. So I'd be curious about yeah, by the point which you have that are actually capable of automating R&D, how are they probably trained?
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。好的。我还有一个问题是，第一批能够自动化 AI 研发的模型实际上将如何训练，因为有一个玩具版本，就是 Ryan 谈到的那个东西，你只是让 GPT-8 尝试构建 GPT-3 大小的模型，这些模型非常擅长像内循环类型的挑战，比如玩需要持续学习的电子游戏，或者用最少的算力达到某个损失值等等。但 John，我认为你有一个有趣的观点，也许那不是实践中实际会发生的方式。所以我很好奇，是的，到你有真正能够自动化研发的模型时，它们可能如何训练？

turns.en: Yeah, I think we'll probably do some combination of learning from human feedback to absorb the researchers' taste and just creating a lot of practice environments which involve doing multi-step research projects. So I think yeah people will in practice do some combination of those two things and just each iteration patch whatever seems to be most broken in the last iteration. So researchers will be using the AIs a lot and we'll notice that they have some consistent weaknesses and then those things will either be patched by collecting human feedback or creating environments.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为我们可能会结合从人类反馈中学习来吸收研究人员的品味，以及创建大量涉及做多步研究项目的练习环境。所以我认为是的，人们实践中会结合这两件事，并且每次迭代修补上一次迭代中最明显的问题。所以研究人员会大量使用 AI，我们会注意到它们有一些一致的弱点，然后这些弱点要么通过收集人类反馈来修补，要么通过创建环境来修补。

turns.en: Yeah. Makes sense.
turns.zh: 是的。有道理。

turns.en: Maybe a useful way to think about this is like how much of the lineage we roll back and then let self-play from there. Like I think in the limit you're picturing just giving them a GPU and maybe neural nets or something and saying okay figure out how to train a model to do these particular tasks.
turns.zh: 也许一个有用的思考方式是，我们回滚多少传承，然后从那里让自我对弈。就像我认为在极限情况下，你想象的是只给他们一个 GPU，也许还有神经网络之类的，然后说：好吧，弄清楚如何训练一个模型来完成这些特定任务。

ts.sec: Training on the frontier of the lineage

turns.en: The way it currently works is we go up to the very edge of the lineage and say, okay, here are the bugs that, you know, Anthropic has found in their training stack in the last few months. Then we turn those into environments: you need to train and get better on the frontier. So you obviously lock in all the previous history of the lineage. But you could imagine a world in which you roll back to, you know, before GRPO or something, and then you have environments that try to get it to discover the best form for, like, reward models, and then maybe roll further and further back. But I think we will still be so compute-bottlenecked that people will just keep staying at the frontier and essentially diffing the bugs and whatever improvements they found since the last model version, turning those into training environments.
turns.zh: 目前的做法是，我们走到这条谱系的最前沿，说：好，这些是 Anthropic 过去几个月在训练栈里发现的 bug。然后把这些变成环境：你需要在前沿上训练、变得更强。所以你显然会锁定谱系里之前的所有历史。但你可以想象一个世界：回滚到比如 GRPO 之前，然后有一些环境试图让它自己发现奖励模型的最佳形式，然后也许再往前回滚。但我认为我们仍然会受算力瓶颈限制，所以人们会一直待在前沿，基本上就是把自上一个模型版本以来发现的 bug 和改进做 diff，把它们变成训练环境。

turns.en: Which is also really good for having non-stale, like, new data between model generations. This is basically continual learning within the AI lab: distilling the last three months of AI research progress through environments and RLHF-type stuff back into the model itself.
turns.zh: 这对在模型代际之间拥有不过时的新数据也很有好处。这基本上就是 AI 实验室内部的持续学习：把过去三个月的 AI 研究进展，通过环境和 RLHF 之类的东西，蒸馏回模型本身。

turns.en: And it is distilling, right? And that's maybe why some of us feel like it's a Sisyphean task: you're always just trying to get the last three months of progress, and that progress is being contributed to by humans, of course, but it also still has humans in the loop. It feels like you're just constantly inching closer and closer to what the human researchers are capable of doing.
turns.zh: 而且这确实是蒸馏，对吧？这也许就是为什么我们有些人觉得这像西西弗斯式的任务：你总是在追赶过去三个月的进展，而那进展当然有人的贡献，但人也仍然在回路里。感觉就像你一直在一点点逼近人类研究者能做到的事情。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: I mean, the one thing I will say though is, obviously, if you're just distilling on trajectories, you can never go above it. But environments can go quite far above what humans can do. It's very easy to design an environment that no human can solve, but the AI can obviously still try and solve it.
turns.zh: 不过我要说的一点是，显然，如果你只是在轨迹上蒸馏，你永远无法超越它。但环境可以远远超出人类能做到的水平。设计一个没人能解决的环境非常容易，但 AI 显然仍然可以尝试去解决它。

turns.en: And so that would be the path to go ahead of just what the human AI research...
turns.zh: 所以那会是一条超越人类 AI 研究水平的路径……

turns.en: Do you have an example of that?
turns.zh: 你有例子吗？

turns.en: In terms of RSI, or like doing it even faster than a human speedrunner?
turns.zh: 是指递归自我改进（RSI），还是比人类速通玩家还快？

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I feel like in AI research especially, it's very easy to define goals where, you know, you could say the loss needs to be 1.3 or something, and no human can get there now, but that's a very extremely measurable, verifiable task, and if the AI gets there, then great, right? I don't know. Building a 100 million parameter model that beats Minecraft, that's maybe too easy, but like a much more complicated game or something.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得尤其在 AI 研究里，定义目标非常容易，比如你可以说损失需要到 1.3 左右，现在没人能达到，但那是一个极其可测量、可验证的任务，如果 AI 达到了，那就太好了，对吧？我不知道。训练一个 1 亿参数的模型打败《我的世界》，那也许太简单了，但换成复杂得多的游戏之类的。

turns.en: Isn't it crazy that 100 million parameter models to beat Minecraft, we're calling that too easy? Like imagine you said that five years ago.
turns.zh: 1 亿参数的模型打败《我的世界》，我们居然说这太简单了，是不是很疯狂？想象一下你五年前说这话。

turns.en: I would say a lot of research is not exactly like that though, where it's like hill climbing on a well-defined goal. It's sort of more like: here's an intuition we have about some way a model should be better, and then we also have some idea for an algorithm that seems to go a little bit in this direction. So let's come up with a task that is sort of designed to show signs of life on this approach, and see if we get those signs of life, and then if we do, we can make successively more realistic versions of the task, right? It's a lot more guided by intuition, and then the inner loop is to elicit or make a test for that intuition, rather than the test itself leading to the insight.
turns.zh: 不过我会说，很多研究并不完全是这样，不是在一个定义明确的目标上爬山。它更像是：我们对模型应该在某个方面更好有一个直觉，然后我们也有一些算法想法，似乎朝这个方向走了一点。所以让我们设计一个任务，用来展示这种方法有生命迹象，看看我们能不能得到那些生命迹象，如果能，我们就可以逐步做出更真实的任务版本，对吧？它更多是由直觉引导的，然后内循环是去引出或为那个直觉做测试，而不是测试本身带来洞见。

turns.en: Right? Like you're not directly optimizing for the eventual objective you care about, or the practical, like, production objective. It's sort of, you're relaxing your objective a little bit. You're saying, yeah, let's relax on the realism axis a little bit and find some methods that actually work, and then try to get back to realism later after the method matures a little bit.
turns.zh: 对吧？你并不是直接优化你最终关心的目标，或者实际的、生产的目标。你是在稍微放松你的目标。你说：好，我们在真实性的轴上稍微放松一点，找到一些真正有效的方法，然后等方法成熟一点再回到真实性。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。

turns.en: And then there's also more research that's more oriented towards explaining things and developing a theory, or a sort of... often we don't have mathematical theories in machine learning that are that predictive, but we have a lot of more informal theories for what's going on.
turns.zh: 然后还有更多研究是更偏向解释事物、发展理论的，或者说……通常我们在机器学习里没有那种很有预测力的数学理论，但我们有很多关于正在发生什么的更非正式的理论。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, presumably the models will be trained on some combination of all of these tasks, and some will be very easily verifiable, some will be like an LLM judge, or just ask the human, does this look reasonable? And then the hope would be that these would all generalize to these much harder, more vague, fuzzy kinds of tasks. And it probably will to some extent. Whether it generalizes enough that the loop can become self-sealing without humans being in the loop at all is unclear.
turns.zh: 是的。我猜模型会在所有这些任务的某种组合上训练，有些非常容易验证，有些像 LLM 裁判，或者直接问人类：这看起来合理吗？然后希望是这些都能泛化到那些难得多、更模糊的任务上。某种程度上大概会。但它是否能泛化到足以让循环在完全没有人类在回路的情况下自我闭合，还不清楚。

turns.en: Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
turns.zh: 是的。是的。是的。

turns.en: Wait, maybe taking a step back. Here's what it seems to me that the plan for AI research going forward is, and you tell me if you think it's going to work or if you agree with this characterization. So the bet is that we will scale up RLVR training across millions of diverse environments across hundreds of different kinds of domains. And what will emerge at the other end is an agent which has learned these basic or less-than-basic skills around being persistent, being able to triage information in context, eventually having end-to-end optimization of working with other agents and things like that. And such an agent will be very sample efficient within the context. You know, you've done research on how you actually scale up in-context learning to make it arbitrarily long, but you keep scaling it up. And so what comes out the other end will be something that basically functions like a drop-in remote worker over the course of a week or a month. First of all, do you agree that that is a bet the labs are making? And second, is that enough, basically learning how to learn within these simulacra within a data center and then getting deployed into the real world, but not actually learning from real-world deployment, only learning these meta skills from the simulated environments in the data center?
turns.zh: 等等，也许退一步说。在我看来，未来 AI 研究的计划是这样的，你告诉我你觉得它会不会奏效，或者你同不同意这个描述。这个赌注是：我们会在数百万个多样化环境、数百种不同领域上扩大 RLVR 训练。另一端涌现出来的会是一个智能体，它学会了这些基本或不太基本的技能：坚持不懈、能在上下文中分诊信息、最终能端到端地优化与其他智能体的协作等等。这样的智能体在上下文内会非常样本高效。你知道，你研究过如何真正扩展上下文学习，让它任意长，但你一直在扩展它。所以另一端出来的东西，基本上会像一个随插即用的远程工作者，能工作一周或一个月。首先，你同意这是实验室正在下的赌注吗？其次，这够吗？基本上就是在数据中心里的这些模拟环境中学会如何学习，然后部署到现实世界，但并不真正从现实世界的部署中学习，只从数据中心的模拟环境里学习这些元技能？

turns.en: Yeah, I think it's now hard to separate out how much of the lab's effort is going towards direct RSI versus making generally intelligent models they can continue to deploy to collect revenue to fund the next big training run. I think for the latter, yes, that's probably just the bet they're making, and it's very clear, like the pattern of where these environments are going over the last few years.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得现在很难区分实验室有多少精力是直接投向 RSI，多少是投向做出可以持续部署、收集收入来资助下一次大训练运行的通用智能模型。我认为对于后者，是的，那大概就是他们正在下的赌注，而且过去几年这些环境的发展模式非常清楚。

turns.en: I mean, Anthropic's lineage of environments is a very clear example of this. First we just focus on coding and we're going to get really, really good at that. Then the task horizon that we've got from coding — which is probably the lowest-hanging fruit in terms of data available on the internet to create environments, their own internal stuff that they can turn into environments — then we're going to generalize. We're going to go after finance next, and literally just so much Excel data and all that sort of stuff in the training. And then, you know, it's PowerPoints. It's this long tail of the working economy. And that seemed to work really well, and a lot of the other labs — even the open-source labs — have now realized that that was the correct approach.
turns.zh: 我是说，Anthropic 的环境谱系就是一个非常清晰的例子。首先我们只专注编程，我们要把这件事做到非常非常好。然后我们从编程中获得的任务时间跨度——这大概是利用互联网上可用数据来构建环境时最容易摘到的果子，还有他们自己内部的东西可以转化成环境——接着我们再去泛化。下一步我们要进军金融，训练数据里literally 有海量的 Excel 数据之类的东西。再然后就是 PowerPoint。这就是工作经济的长尾。这似乎效果非常好，很多其他实验室——甚至开源实验室——现在都意识到那才是正确的做法。

turns.en: But what is the implication from that? When I had Dario on the podcast, the thing I asked him was: if you truly expect models which will be humanlike in their ability to learn on the job, why would you try to bake in all these skills of like working with PowerPoint or something? Wouldn't you just expect the model to be able to pick that up while it's deployed?
turns.zh: 但那意味着什么呢？我请 Dario 上播客时，我问他的问题是：如果你真的期望模型在学习能力上像人一样、能在工作中学习，那你为什么还要把这些比如用 PowerPoint 之类的技能预先烘焙进去呢？你难道不会期望模型在部署之后自己就能学会这些吗？

turns.en: Yeah, there's multiple different explanations. One is just that we expect models to get there soon, but they're not there yet. So why not amortize these skills into the model training? Another is that we're not concentrated on making it really good at widely deployed work. We just want it really good at RSI. And this is just a way for us to get revenue so that we can pour it back into a model that is actually really good at doing RSI development. And then once the singularity happens, the thing that comes out the other end will be really good at all the things which seem like bottlenecks to the current generation of models.
turns.zh: 对，有几种不同的解释。一种是我们预期模型很快就能达到那个水平，但现在还没到。那为什么不把这些技能摊销进模型训练里呢？另一种是我们并不专注于让它把广泛部署的工作做得很好。我们只想让它把 RSI 做得很好。而这只是我们获取收入的一种方式，好把钱再投回一个真正擅长做 RSI 开发的模型里。然后一旦奇点发生，最终出来的那个东西会在当前这一代模型看起来是瓶颈的所有事情上都非常擅长。

turns.en: Yeah, John, I don't know if you have takes on how — once you construe why there is so much task-specific knowledge in these models — if the path is this kind of generalization.
turns.zh: 对，John，不知道你有没有看法：如果路径是这种泛化，那你怎么解释这些模型里为什么有这么多任务特定的知识？

turns.en: Yeah, I mean, if the models were good enough at learning in context, then in theory you wouldn't need to train them on finance. They would just be able to figure out — read all the books on the fly and figure out how to do everything in the appropriate jurisdiction.
turns.zh: 对，我是说，如果模型在上下文学习方面足够好，那理论上你就不需要用金融数据训练它们。它们就能自己搞定——当场读完所有书，然后弄清楚如何在相应的司法管辖区里做每一件事。

turns.en: Um, yeah, and you could argue that you need to do a lot of this domain-specific training just to make them more efficient. So even if they were smart enough to figure this out on the fly, you still might want to do a bunch of RL and bake all these intuitions into the weights, so the model would be more efficient at runtime.
turns.zh: 嗯，对，你也可以说，你需要做大量这种领域特定的训练，只是为了让他们更高效。所以即使它们聪明到能当场想明白，你可能还是想做一堆强化学习，把这些直觉烘焙进权重里，这样模型在推理时会更高效。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Yeah. I'd say in practice it does seem like model providers are going domain by domain and trying to strengthen the models in the highest-value domain. And I'd say that's one of the answers to why the models have gotten so much better. It's just because the model providers have covered a lot of the high-value domains and the most common types of skills.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得在实践中，模型提供方确实是一个领域一个领域地推进，努力在最高价值的领域强化模型。我觉得这也是模型为什么变得好这么多的答案之一。就是因为模型提供方覆盖了很多高价值领域和最常用的技能类型。

turns.en: I mean, I think another thing is just that it's not that expensive to do both at the same time, right? Because the models are massive. They can easily afford, in terms of their parameters, to learn everything. And there is likely some transfer — even if finance is not specifically important for RSI, just the general meta-learning of how to figure out what's important, how to have taste, how to do long-horizon work, is potentially generalizable. And there's not that much RSI data in the world as well. It's kind of hard to generate and requires a lot of effort. So if you can amortize in this other data, get some transfer from it — you already have masses of compute, masses of parameter space — why not do that as well as the obvious direct commercial incentive of selling a model?
turns.zh: 我是说，我觉得另一点是，同时做这两件事其实没那么贵，对吧？因为模型非常庞大。就参数量而言，它们很容易负担得起学会一切。而且很可能存在一些迁移——即使金融对 RSI 不是特别重要，光是那种通用的元学习：如何判断什么重要、如何有品味、如何做长跨度的工作，这些都可能具有泛化性。而且世界上并没有那么多 RSI 数据，它挺难生成的，需要大量投入。所以如果你能把这些其他数据摊销进来、从中获得一些迁移——你本来就有海量算力、海量参数空间——那为什么不也这么做呢？再加上卖模型这个显而易见的直接商业激励。

turns.en: Yeah, it makes sense.
turns.zh: 对，有道理。

turns.en: Oh yeah, I'll add that. I mean, there's one question about whether this current paradigm of doing sim-to-real will be the dominant one forever. So basically you look at what the real-world tasks are like, and then you try to create a bunch of environments that can be simulated in the data center, and you can do RL on them. And I think obviously this has been very successful, but it has a lot of weaknesses, because a lot of things are just kind of hard to simulate, especially if they involve interacting with a bunch of humans in real time. Yeah. So there's some question about whether sim-to-real will be the dominant framework forever.

turns.en: Jane Street just launched a new competition and it's their most ambitious one yet: design a protocol emulator ASIC. Basically, if you have a chip that you want to test, you can connect it to this ASIC and then this ASIC will simulate realistic traffic. That way you can see how the chip responds without having to plug it into a live system. Jane Street is looking for flexible, general-purpose designs, not single-protocol emulators. When I was chatting with them, they suggested that I start off by trying to implement what are apparently three very common protocols: UART, SPI, and I2C. Jere also mentioned that they hoped more ambitious designs will also tackle low-speed USB and Ethernet and any other protocols that flex your chip-specific architecture. Importantly, your design should be reprogrammable rather than smashing a bunch of specific protocols onto a chip. If a new protocol comes out after your ASIC is taped out, your chip still needs to be able to handle it. How exactly it does it is up to you, but there is one hard constraint: your design must target an open-source 130 nm process node. That's because Jane Street will pay to tape out the most novel submissions and send the physical copies to the winners. The competition is open till January 18th, 2027, and working in teams is highly encouraged.
turns.zh: Jane Street 刚刚推出了一项新竞赛，这是他们迄今最有野心的一次：设计一款协议仿真器 ASIC。基本上，如果你有一块想测试的芯片，你可以把它连接到这块 ASIC 上，然后这块 ASIC 会模拟真实的流量。这样你就能看到芯片如何响应，而无需把它插进一个真实系统里。Jane Street 想要的是灵活、通用的设计，而不是单一协议的仿真器。我和他们聊的时候，他们建议我先从实现三种据说非常常见的协议开始：UART、SPI 和 I2C。Jere 还提到，他们希望更有野心的设计也能处理低速 USB 和以太网，以及任何其他能考验你芯片特定架构的协议。重要的是，你的设计应当是可重新编程的，而不是把一堆特定协议硬砸到一块芯片上。如果你的 ASIC 流片之后出现了一种新协议，你的芯片仍然需要能够处理它。具体怎么实现由你决定，但有一个硬性约束：你的设计必须针对开源的 130 纳米工艺节点。这是因为 Jane Street 会为最新颖的提交付费流片，并把实物寄给获胜者。竞赛开放至 2027 年 1 月 18 日，非常鼓励组队参加。

turns.en: I think maybe the way I'd break down the two types of tasks in which models get good and models will still continue to struggle is whether the task is cumulative or whether you kind of have this non-stationary distribution where you have to keep learning and relitigating a bunch of stuff. If it's true that for RSI we don't need to discover a new attention variant or whatever—once you've discovered attention, and once you've discovered mixture of experts, and once you discover GPO, you just add that to the training stack and that's there. So that's an example of a cumulative task. I think the real world—and the reason people are thinking so much about continual learning—is it's not really a cumulative task. Imagine in a law firm you have an agent acting as a legal associate. That's a very non-stationary distribution. You have to be able to fit in your context all the relationships between all the important people at that company, which are also changing all the time.

turns.en: Yeah, I would say today's models are weaker than humans in a lot of different ways, and some of them might have to do with sample efficiency in a certain regime. In some regimes models are very sample efficient, like learning in context. But then there might be some medium-length regime where they're less sample efficient because humans can do some kind of weight update more efficiently than models. So I think being less sample efficient in certain regimes might be one of the sources of weakness. But then I think there are other sources of weakness that are completely different from that—for example, having lower diversity of thought than humans, or being bad at certain kinds of long-horizon judgments. I mean, I think a lot of what people call taste is something about behavior that works in the long run and that people have realized works in the long run. Not everything, but some aspect of taste—especially for something like software engineering—I think a lot of taste is about what are the systems that are going to be maintainable and work well in the long run of this project. So yeah, I think the weaknesses of humans which limit RSI, along with other things, are a variety of them, and some of them are related to sample efficiency and some aren't.
