turns.zh: 嗯，我的意思是，它必须被训练成能从那个上下文中学习。所以我不确定——要么它必须被训练成能从那个上下文中做出正确的更新，要么——

turns.en: You have to just dump it all in—like your whole life, your whole research experience.
turns.zh: 你得把全部东西都倒进去——比如你的一生、你全部的科研经历。

turns.en: I mean, you still need the data to train it long context, right? Even if you could theoretically get a trillion context, you would need a trillion lengths of data to train it. Like right now you have like context—
turns.zh: 我的意思是，你仍然需要数据来训练它的长上下文，对吧？即使理论上你能获得一万亿的上下文，你也需要一万亿长度的数据来训练它。就像现在你有上下文——

turns.en: I'm just asking if you had that in theory.
turns.zh: 我只是在问，理论上如果你有那个的话。

turns.en: I think yes. I mean, this really just comes down to the question of how meta-learnable taste is from shorter-horizon episodes. And I feel like there's no obvious reason it's super long, because humans somehow develop taste without having many long episodes—like we don't live to be 10,000.
turns.zh: 我觉得答案是肯定的。我的意思是，这真的就归结为一个问题：品味从较短时程的片段中有多强的元可学习性。我觉得没有明显理由说它必须超级长，因为人类不知怎么就在没有很多长片段的情况下发展出了品味——我们又不是活到一万岁。

ts.sec: Developing Taste and Learning from Deployment

turns.en: We develop pretty quickly, right? And so if you think about even in a PhD, the difference between a first-year PhD student and a final postdoc or something, that's like five years maybe, and they've only done maybe 10, 15, 30 research projects in total, but somehow they develop taste quite quickly from a relatively short succession of small things. And so theoretically it's possible to develop it like that. The AI obviously will have vastly more experience in which to develop taste, to meta-learn it. And how well does that generalize to really long-horizon things is I think the question which is really unsolved at this point. Like we don't know. Going back to this question, eventually there should be a regime where AIs are learning a ton from each individual instance of deployment. Well, currently you could say there's a meta fuzzy process by which models do improve from deployment, but I feel like it's a very weak feedback loop.
turns.zh: 我们发展得很快，对吧？所以如果你想想，即使在博士阶段，一个一年级博士生和一个最后的博士后之间的差距，那大概是五年，他们总共可能只做了 10、15、30 个研究项目，但不知何故他们从相对短暂的一系列小事中很快培养出了品味。所以理论上是有可能这样培养的。AI 显然会有多得多的经验来培养品味，来元学习它。而这在多大程度上能泛化到真正长视野的事情上，我认为是目前真正未解决的问题。我们不知道。回到这个问题，最终应该有一个阶段，AI 从每次部署的实例中学到大量东西。目前你可以说有一个元模糊过程，模型确实从部署中改进，但我觉得这是一个非常弱的反馈回路。

turns.en: Do you see this around the horizon where there's this hive mind kind of learning that's very rapid? And if so, how exactly does it happen?
turns.zh: 你看到这种快速学习的蜂巢思维即将出现了吗？如果是，它究竟如何发生？

turns.en: Actually I would say that around will we get a hive mind that learns from all of its deployment experience? I mean a big part of that is actually about incentives rather than being a technical question. So companies aren't going to want to have the model provider learn from all of their deployment because that might just reduce the advantage of their business.
turns.zh: 实际上我想说，关于我们是否会得到一个从所有部署经验中学习的蜂巢思维？其中很大一部分实际上是关于激励，而不是技术问题。所以公司不会希望模型提供商从他们所有的部署中学习，因为那可能只会降低他们业务的优势。

turns.en: I think that maybe the economics of this will pressure not necessarily weight updates to one big common shared model but kind of modules that get subbed in. Like a very obvious example, this is a LoRA, but it might be something else. Like you know there's been a lot of work to try and fit an arbitrary context length into a fixed size, like this is all the linear attention stuff and all that sort of stuff, and like cartridges which are essentially KV caches trained to be very very compressed KV caches to fit in a lot of information. That's another example of something that companies may be willing to sign up for if that gets subbed into the model and it's not actually changing the base underlying model itself. So like there's many different versions of learning from your data in real time, and the latter ones are not really helping the big labs because they are just these modules. But I think the economic pressure will force the labs to go down that path first before they can embark on this.
turns.zh: 我认为也许经济因素会迫使不是对一个大共享模型进行权重更新，而是某种模块被替换进来。一个很明显的例子是 LoRA，但也可能是别的。你知道有很多工作试图将任意上下文长度适配到固定大小，比如所有线性注意力之类的东西，还有像“卡带”这样的东西，本质上是训练成非常非常压缩的 KV 缓存，以容纳大量信息。这是另一个例子，公司可能愿意接受，如果它被替换到模型中，而实际上并不改变底层基础模型本身。所以有很多不同版本的从数据中实时学习，而后面的那些并不真正帮助大实验室，因为它们只是这些模块。但我认为经济压力会迫使实验室先走这条路，然后才能开始这个。

turns.en: So which economic pressure though? Because I feel like even if you have a bunch of cartridges or LoRAs or whatnot, you can still just take all these traces and just distill this down to the pre-training of your next generation of models.
turns.zh: 但究竟是哪种经济压力？因为我觉得即使你有一堆卡带或 LoRA 之类的，你仍然可以拿走所有这些轨迹，然后将其蒸馏到你下一代模型的预训练中。

turns.en: Yeah. So it may be a more indirect form of learning that the big labs are getting, and that's obviously still really valuable to them, but I can't imagine a world in which we start off with like, you know, we're going to just directly train this one big model on all the exact data. I think it will definitely go through stages because this is assuming there's one discontinuous event whereas suddenly we fix weight updates continuously, and in practice I think it's much more likely to be like the cartridges and stuff allow you to specialize in deployments, then you generate traces, you put that in your model, like 3 months later you come out with a model which is better at this stuff, you specialize it again and you consolidate it again, and then eventually we'll just make this loop faster and faster. So instead of every 3 months we release a model, now it's like every week and then every day and then every hour, at which point we basically have obviously solved it.
turns.zh: 是的。所以大实验室获得的可能是一种更间接的学习形式，这显然对他们仍然非常有价值，但我无法想象一个世界，我们从一开始就说，我们要直接在一个大模型上训练所有精确数据。我认为它肯定会经历阶段，因为这是假设有一个不连续的事件，突然我们连续地修复权重更新，而在实践中，我认为更可能是这样的：卡带之类的东西让你在部署中专业化，然后你生成轨迹，你把它放入你的模型，比如 3 个月后你推出一个在这方面更好的模型，你再次专业化并再次巩固，然后最终我们会让这个循环越来越快。所以不是每 3 个月发布一个模型，现在是每周，然后每天，然后每小时，到那时我们基本上显然已经解决了它。

turns.en: Yeah, and I think this is a good point as well because you asked kind of how far off the current paradigm we are from being able to do this. I think we've done a bit of research to this and people have done a lot of research at a really large scale. Like when you wash out enough noise and you have large enough batches, like this outer loop process of putting data into mid-training and creating our environments, like it does work in some sort of continual learning regime. But the problem is when you zoom in close enough at a micro level, it's like I've got one model and I'm trying to update it again for a law firm or something. And I'm trying to do that very continuously with a relatively small amount of data. Like all the methods kind of break down a bit. So like if I SFT the model on just successful traces, off-policy, on-policy, like eventually in the very iterative regime, when you're doing hundreds of these micro updates, you see both catastrophic forgetting, you see forgetting of previous information I've learned on top of the base model that was much earlier on, and I see degradation of general capabilities. You know, on-policy distillation seems to push this horizon out a little bit but it still eventually succumbs to the same. And RL is not very good at—it is good at getting capabilities in, but it's not as good as getting knowledge in, and just this very explicit knowledge of like, oh okay, this person does this at this law firm and this is a very specific process we find, and you have to pour in a lot of compute to create the right environments to get the knowledge in.
turns.zh: 是的，我认为这也是一个好观点，因为你问的是我们离能够做到这一点有多远。我想我们对此做了一些研究，人们也在非常大的规模上做了很多研究。就像当你洗掉足够的噪声并且有足够大的批次时，这种将数据放入中期训练并创建我们的环境的外循环过程，它确实在某种持续学习机制中起作用。但问题是，当你放大到微观层面时，就像我有一个模型，我试图再次为一家律师事务所更新它。我试图非常连续地用相对少量的数据来做这件事。就像所有方法都有点崩溃。所以如果我仅对成功的轨迹进行 SFT，离策略、在策略，最终在非常迭代的机制中，当你进行数百次这样的微更新时，你会看到灾难性遗忘，你会看到对之前我在基础模型之上学到的信息的遗忘，并且我看到一般能力的退化。你知道，在策略蒸馏似乎将这一视野推远了一点，但它最终仍然屈服于同样的问题。而强化学习不太擅长——它擅长获取能力，但不那么擅长获取知识，以及这种非常明确的知识，比如，哦好吧，这个人在这个律师事务所做这个，这是我们发现的一个非常具体的过程，你必须投入大量算力来创建正确的环境以获取知识。

turns.en: Do you think that the fundamental issue here—why you get worse at any of these other skills or there's forgetting and stuff—do you think it's fundamentally an issue of capacity or it's an issue of techniques?
turns.zh: 你认为这里的根本问题——为什么你在任何这些其他技能上变差，或者有遗忘之类的——你认为这根本上是容量问题还是技术问题？

turns.en: A little bit of both, I think. Like SFT and even distillation, like on-policy distillation, can be way too destructive. The reason RL is so nice is because it changes a very very small amount about the model, and there's a lot of evidence for why this is the case, and so it kind of just tweaks it in this very very small loss value to get it into the right point. But that also then limits what you can do with RL, like how much you can actually change the model.
turns.zh: 我认为两者都有一点。就像 SFT 甚至蒸馏，比如在策略蒸馏，可能破坏性太大。强化学习之所以好，是因为它对模型的改变非常非常小，有很多证据表明为什么是这样，所以它只是在这个非常非常小的损失值上调整它，使其达到正确的点。但这也限制了你能用强化学习做什么，比如你实际上能改变模型多少。

turns.en: Or sorry, are you saying like the reason this isn't a winner-take-all potentially is that it's just very hard to distill that much information into the base model without ruining something in the interface?
turns.zh: 或者抱歉，你是说这之所以可能不是赢家通吃，是因为很难在不破坏接口中的某些东西的情况下将那么多信息蒸馏到基础模型中？

turns.en: Like it's easy to distill it into a different base model. Like this is where I think it's mostly technique. It's definitely not just like there isn't capacity.
turns.zh: 就像将其蒸馏到一个不同的基础模型是容易的。我认为这主要是技术问题。这绝对不只是容量不够。

turns.en: Like if you had some model with all this data, and you take literally the same size model and pre-train it from scratch with all of this stuff in mid-training, it will be better. And I think that's a lot of what's happening today.
turns.zh: 比如你有一个模型，带着所有这些数据，然后你拿一个完全相同规模的模型，用所有这些内容在中期训练里从头预训练，它会更好。我觉得今天发生的很多事情就是这样。

turns.en: Yeah. And so it's very much like there's a bottleneck that stops us from just keeping training the same model forever, versus just getting all the data from the old model and training a new model from scratch. And this is exactly saying some combination of plasticity and catastrophic forgetting—if you just naively train on non-stationary data because you're adding new data as you go, basically this is messing with the data distribution. So the old stuff is just forgotten, and we don't really have good methods to stop that from happening.
turns.zh: 对。所以很大程度上是有一个瓶颈，阻止我们一直训练同一个模型，而不是把旧模型的所有数据拿出来、从头训练一个新模型。这说的正是可塑性和灾难性遗忘的某种组合——如果你只是天真地在非平稳数据上训练，因为你一边训练一边加入新数据，这基本上就是在扰乱数据分布。于是旧的东西就被遗忘了，而我们并没有真正好的方法来阻止这种情况发生。

turns.en: And so maybe in the limit you're just bottlenecked by retraining the model from scratch with all this new information.
turns.zh: 所以也许在极限情况下，你就是被“用所有这些新信息从头重训模型”这件事卡住了。

turns.en: Yes. Which of course is very expensive—training a model from scratch is expensive.
turns.zh: 对。这当然非常昂贵——从头训练一个模型很贵。

turns.en: But you're going to do that anyways.
turns.zh: 但反正你都会这么做。

turns.en: I mean, not necessarily. Maybe eventually, if you have continual learning, you never train a new model—you just have a model and it keeps learning and expanding, right?
turns.zh: 我的意思是，不一定。也许最终，如果你有持续学习，你就永远不训练新模型——你只有一个模型，它不断学习和扩展，对吧？

turns.en: But there might be some deep technical reason why that's very difficult because of these—
turns.zh: 但可能有一些深层技术原因让这非常困难，因为这些——

turns.en: I mean, that's the question. I think we have pushed back on how much from scratch we need to do. It is definitely possible now to take the pre-trained base and do very good mid-training on top of that, kind of continuously, plus some RL from different checkpoints that are later on in the training, and that's looking more like learning. But certainly not the case of taking the most recent model, applying a couple of very small updates, and iteratively never losing it.
turns.zh: 我的意思是，这就是问题所在。我觉得我们已经在“需要多少从头训练”这件事上往回推了。现在完全可能拿预训练基座，在上面做非常好的中期训练，某种程度上是持续的，再加上从训练后期不同检查点出发的一些强化学习，这看起来更像学习了。但肯定不是那种拿最新模型、做几次很小的更新、然后迭代地永不丢失的情况。

turns.en: But isn't this—I'm a bit confused, because isn't this literally what happens during training, where during post-training or something you just have a model that's already gone through so much training, and then you distill some fork that's been further RL'd or something? Isn't that literally what happens?
turns.zh: 但这不是——我有点困惑，因为这难道不就是训练过程中发生的事吗？在后训练之类的阶段，你有一个已经经过大量训练的模型，然后你蒸馏某个经过进一步强化学习的分支之类的？这不就是实际发生的事吗？

turns.en: It's still at a large enough scale, I think, that you're washing out a lot of the noise, and you're not just focused on one distribution—which, as Beren said, is now very much—if you're just focusing on one task, right? In the eventual regime you'd be doing, I don't know, there's billions of deployed instances, you're learning from all of them at once, and so hopefully there's some washing out of noise and stuff from that, right?
turns.zh: 我觉得它仍然处在足够大的规模上，所以你会洗掉很多噪声，而且你不是只专注于一个分布——正如 Beren 所说，现在非常——如果你只专注于一个任务，对吧？在最终的状态下你会做的是，我不知道，有数十亿个部署实例，你同时从所有这些实例中学习，所以希望这能洗掉一些噪声之类的东西，对吧？

turns.en: Maybe at that scale. Yeah.
turns.zh: 也许在那个规模上。对。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think definitely, as I was saying, you can do continual mid-training for a long time, and you can roll back to a checkpoint and give new mid-training data. But at the same time, you can't do this indefinitely—if you just keep continuing mid-training the same base forever, it sort of asymptotes. You can't just learn new stuff in that base, and this is why people end up training new bases. Otherwise you would just keep mid-training the same base forever.
turns.zh: 对。我的意思是，我觉得确实，就像我说的，你可以做很长时间的持续中期训练，也可以回滚到某个检查点、喂入新的中期训练数据。但与此同时，你不能无限地这么做——如果你就一直对同一个基座持续中期训练下去，它某种程度上会渐近饱和。你没法在那个基座里学到新东西，这就是为什么人们最终会训练新的基座。否则你就只会一直中期训练同一个基座。

turns.en: Whenever I finish recording an interview, I immediately brain dump all my thoughts into Slack—things like what was most interesting and what should get cut. This ensures that my editors have all the context they need to start editing the episode. But it's not like these brain dumps have any clear timestamps, and my unedited recordings are many hours long. It can take a ton of editor time to even find the exact moments that I was referencing. So we decided to try adding a Grok Bot producer to our chat. Now, whenever one of my editors posts a rough cut of the episode, Grok Bot opens a transcript on its own computer and starts working, usually before I've even seen the message. It takes the notes that I dropped into Slack and highlights the relevant snippets in the transcript. It also uses a big case file that I've compiled with all my preferences so it can suggest potential edits. And when it's done, it sends me its top clip candidates so that I can review everything from my phone. This has worked really well. Being able to send informal messages like I'm texting my editor and then having the transcript immediately reflect my preferences has just been so helpful. Try Grok Bot yourself at x.ai/bot.
turns.zh: 每次我录完一场访谈，我都会立刻把所有想法一股脑倒进 Slack——比如什么最有意思、什么该剪掉。这能确保我的编辑们拿到开始剪辑这期节目所需的全部背景。但这些脑暴笔记并没有清晰的时间戳，而我没剪过的录音长达好几个小时。光是找到我提到的那些确切片段，就可能耗费编辑大量时间。所以我们决定试着往聊天里加一个 Grok Bot 制作人。现在，只要我的某位编辑发出这期节目的粗剪版，Grok Bot 就会在它自己的电脑上打开转录稿开始干活，通常在我看到消息之前就开始了。它会拿我丢进 Slack 的笔记，在转录稿里高亮出相关片段。它还会用我整理的一份包含我所有偏好的大案例文件，来给出可能的剪辑建议。做完之后，它会把它最看好的候选片段发给我，让我能在手机上审阅全部内容。这招效果非常好。能像给编辑发短信一样发些非正式消息，然后转录稿立刻反映出我的偏好，真是太有用了。你可以自己在 x.ai/bot 试试 Grok Bot。

turns.en: Okay, let's talk a bit about data now. So I'm generally interested in this question of how much of AI progress is just explained by data progress. Doesn't mean it will necessarily be hard to automate, but that's a separate question. So is there some data distribution which, if you trained current architectures on, would result in a superintelligence that totally dominates human experts across every single field?
turns.zh: 好，我们现在聊一聊数据。我总体上对这个问题很感兴趣：AI 的进步有多少只是由数据进步解释的。这并不意味着它一定难以自动化，但那是另一个问题。那么，是否存在某种数据分布，如果你用当前架构在它上面训练，就会得到一个在每个领域都完全碾压人类专家的超级智能？

turns.en: Are we talking about pre-training plus post-training data, like environments as well? I think the existence of this is obvious. It's just whether we can create the right environments.
turns.zh: 我们说的是预训练加后训练数据，也包括环境吗？我觉得这种东西的存在是显而易见的。问题只在于我们能否造出正确的环境。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: In the trivial case, we could just train it to output the Python file which trains the actual superintelligence—just have that memorizing the weights.
turns.zh: 在最简单的情况下，我们可以直接训练它输出那个训练出真正超级智能的 Python 文件——就让它记住那些权重。

turns.en: Like yes, there's probably a ladder of environments that it's possible to construct such that you would get an AI researcher which is at least as good as a human researcher. But the effort to climb each successive rung grows kind of exponentially. And that's going to be the two things that you have to trade off against as to how fast we're going to hit that final rung where it's better. I think that's fairly clear. And I think we're still relatively early in our environment creation. There's a lot of asymmetries that we exploit in order to create good environments. So one of those asymmetries, which we've talked about before, is that there are environments where it's easier to go backwards and forwards. And what I mean by that is it's very easy to define this complex data generating process, and this is like this kind of latent variable you keep hidden from the model. You can generate arbitrarily complex environments, and the model has to do a lot of irreducible token spend and irreducible work to figure out what that data generating process was. There's asymmetries in terms of you can inject information from the real world.
turns.zh: 是的，可能存在一个可以构造出来的环境阶梯，让你得到一个至少和人类研究员一样好的 AI 研究员。但每往上爬一级，所需的努力大致呈指数增长。而这两件事就是你必须权衡的，以判断我们多快能到达最后那一级、也就是它更好的那一级。我觉得这一点相当清楚。而且我认为我们在环境创造方面还相对早期。我们利用了很多不对称性来创造好的环境。其中一个不对称性，我们之前聊过，就是有些环境更容易正推和反推。我的意思是，定义一个复杂的数据生成过程非常容易，这就像你向模型隐藏的一个潜变量。你可以生成任意复杂的环境，而模型必须花费大量不可削减的 token 和不可削减的工作，才能弄清楚那个数据生成过程是什么。还有一些不对称性，比如你可以从真实世界注入信息。

turns.en: So Anthropic finds a bug through tens of thousands of human and LMR hours combined, and turns that into a very, very neat environment which a single LM could theoretically find within a few million tokens. So there are all these asymmetries which we're cherry-picking, and we're counting on this task-horizon generalization. But I think, again, there are just going to be diminishing returns at some point—diminishing returns in how hard it is to create those environments in the first place, like coming up with them, because you can't necessarily just have these processes where it's easier to go backwards than forwards. You actually have to sit down and construct something that, with humans, looks like a long enough time horizon—it's going to be a really complex task to create. And then there are also going to be the compute and time bottlenecks for the agent to actually do those tasks. So I think you're just going to start seeing this curve flatten out.
turns.zh: Anthropic 通过结合数万小时的人工和 LMR 时间发现了一个 bug，然后把它变成一个非常非常精巧的环境，单个语言模型理论上可以在几百万个 token 内找到它。所以我们 cherry-pick 了所有这些不对称性，并指望这种任务视野上的泛化。但我觉得，同样地，某个时候一定会出现收益递减——在创建这些环境本身的难度上出现收益递减，比如想出这些环境，因为你不一定能直接拥有这些过程，让倒退比前进更容易。你实际上必须坐下来构建某种东西，对人类来说，它看起来像是一个足够长的时间视野——创建它将会是一项非常复杂的任务。然后还有智能体实际执行这些任务时的算力和时间瓶颈。所以我觉得你只会开始看到这条曲线变平。

turns.en: I saw something about how someone fine-tuned the Talkie model—which is only trained on data up to 1930—on modern coding-agent data, and it did better than Claude 3 Opus on SWE-bench. So this model that has no knowledge of code whatsoever can be fine-tuned on a moderate amount of data and behave better as a coding agent than this much larger pre-trained model—that's pretty crazy. And it kind of shows you that once you have an example of the right expert behavior, it's actually surprisingly easy to copy that into a relatively weak model.
turns.zh: 我看到过一些东西，说有人把 Talkie 模型——它只训练到 1930 年的数据——在现代编码智能体数据上做了微调，结果它在 SWE-bench 上比 Claude 3 Opus 表现更好。所以这个完全不懂代码的模型，可以在适量数据上微调，然后作为编码智能体表现得比这个大得多的预训练模型更好——这挺疯狂的。这也多少说明，一旦你有了正确专家行为的例子，把它复制到一个相对较弱的模型里其实出奇地容易。

turns.en: Yeah. But a counterexample to that is there was a paper recently where they trained it up to fifth-grade maths, and also like primary-school English and stuff. So it was a decent language model, and they tried to RL it to do late high-school and college maths, and the gap was just too large. They couldn't get it to climb at all. But if you did successive runs—like year-seven maths, then year-eight maths, and so on—you could obviously climb to year 12. So again, it's just: what is the distance between the rungs on those ladders, and how hard is it to create?
turns.zh: 是的。但一个反例是，最近有一篇论文，他们把它训练到五年级数学，还有小学英语之类的。所以它是一个还不错的语言模型，然后他们试着用强化学习让它做高中后期和大学数学，差距实在太大了。他们根本没法让它爬上去。但如果你做连续的训练——比如七年级数学，然后八年级数学，以此类推——你显然可以爬到十二年级。所以 again，问题就是：那些梯子上的横档之间距离有多远，以及创建它们有多难？

turns.en: Yeah. And this just comes back to the RL signal problem. RL is not very good at exploring right now. So if the model can't get in, you know, 128 rollouts, it's very unlikely to get signal to progress. And this is why in RL we need curricula, whereas in pre-training we don't, because that's not a problem for pre-training at all.
turns.zh: 是的。这就回到了强化学习信号的问题。强化学习现在不太擅长探索。所以如果模型在 128 次 rollout 里都找不到，它极不可能获得进展的信号。这就是为什么在强化学习中我们需要课程，而在预训练中我们不需要，因为这对预训练来说根本不是问题。

turns.en: Yeah. And again, pre-training data is different from post-training data. And I imagine as we continue on, humans will be involved less and less, but that doesn't change the fact that you're bottlenecked on how much signal you can extract from the real world. So there's a lot of signal in the world—that's true, there are people doing spreadsheet tasks, people doing legal tasks and all this sort of stuff—but the capability frontier of where the models are at now: how many bits in the world are actually really relevant to improving the model's capabilities? How many new maths problems are being solved that are just beyond the reach or grasp of the current models? How many new coding problems are being created or solved that are beyond the reach of the current models? And I think that's why the diminishing returns kicks in, because even the world as a whole is not giving you the bits that are useful for tipping you into the next basin of capability.
turns.zh: 是的。而且 again，预训练数据和后训练数据是不同的。我想随着我们继续推进，人类的参与会越来越少，但这不改变一个事实：你受限于能从真实世界提取多少信号。世界上有很多信号——这是真的，有人在处理电子表格任务，有人在处理法律任务等等——但模型现在所处的能力前沿：世界上有多少比特实际上真正与提升模型能力相关？有多少新的数学问题正在被解决，而这些问题超出了当前模型的能力范围或理解范围？有多少新的编码问题正在被创造或解决，而它们超出了当前模型的能力范围？我觉得这就是收益递减出现的原因，因为即使整个世界也没有给你那些有用的比特，把你推入下一个能力盆地。

turns.en: Yeah, I totally agree with this. So it's really a question of where the signal is coming from. In pre-training, the signal is already in Common Crawl, right? For the tasks you care about in pre-training, the problem is not just getting signal at all—it's filtering out all the noise that exists, and that's quite an automatable process. But as the models get better, as we enter mid-training and post-training, the signal just doesn't exist anywhere in the original data. No amount of filtering will get this—there's no hidden proof of the Millennium Prize problem sitting in Common Crawl that we can just filter until we see it. And so at that point you have to get bits some other way: either from humans directly, like asking them to write out their reasoning, or by creating environments where humans decide what environment should be created and what the objectives of these environments are, or some kind of training on the human data that exists in deployment. You have to get the bits from somewhere.
turns.zh: 是的，我完全同意。所以这真的是信号来自哪里的问题。在预训练中，信号已经在 Common Crawl 里了，对吧？对于预训练中你关心的任务，问题根本不是获取信号——而是过滤掉所有存在的噪声，而这是一个相当可自动化的过程。但随着模型变得更好，随着我们进入中期训练和后训练，信号在原始数据里根本不存在。再多的过滤也得不到——Common Crawl 里没有隐藏的千禧年大奖难题的证明，让我们可以一直过滤直到看见它。所以到那个时候，你必须以其他方式获取比特：要么直接来自人类，比如让他们写出推理过程；要么通过创建环境，由人类决定应该创建什么环境以及这些环境的目标是什么；要么在部署中存在的真实人类数据上进行某种训练。你必须从某个地方获取比特。

turns.en: Yeah. There's a question of how much of the progress in pre-training is being driven by data.
turns.zh: 是的。有一个问题是，预训练中有多少进展是由数据驱动的。

turns.en: I did this investigation with Jerry Han, who's a student at Princeton, where we basically trained all the recipes from 2019 till now pairwise with all the data sets from 2019 to now. So you train GPT-2 on the newest data set, like UltraFineWeb, and you train Dolly—which is the newest training recipe, or the open-source training recipe—on the Pile or some old data set, and you do the whole grid, and you see getting to some level of capabilities: how much less compute does it take across this grid? And you see that the data seems to explain like a 9x compute efficiency gain, but the architecture improvements explain like a 3x compute efficiency gain at a very small scale. And so, to the extent that that is true at large scale—that most of the pre-training compute efficiency gains are coming from better data—how much can that continue? Can you keep just filtering data more and more and building more and more synthetic data until... yeah, do you have a sense of how much this kind of pre-training progress can continue?
turns.zh: 我和 Jerry Han——普林斯顿的一个学生——做了这项研究，我们基本上把 2019 年至今的所有训练配方与 2019 年至今的所有数据集两两配对训练。所以你在最新的数据集比如 UltraFineWeb 上训练 GPT-2，然后在 Pile 或某个旧数据集上训练 Dolly——它是最新的训练配方，或者说开源训练配方——你跑完整个网格，看达到某个能力水平需要多少更少的算力。你发现数据似乎解释了大约 9 倍的算力效率提升，而架构改进在非常小的规模上解释了大约 3 倍的算力效率提升。所以，如果这在大规模下也成立——即预训练算力效率提升的大部分来自更好的数据——那这能持续多久？你能一直越来越多地过滤数据、构建越来越多的合成数据，直到……是的，你对这种预训练进展能持续多久有感觉吗？

turns.en: I think my prior is that, again, the low-hanging fruit is somewhat exhausted. We got the internet as this big block, and the internet isn't necessarily growing at the same rate—all the useful stuff on the internet is growing at the same rate. So we've probably got a bunch of like 0.1% loss drops to go, but definitely not as many as have currently occurred.
turns.zh: 我觉得我的先验是，again，低垂的果实某种程度上已经摘完了。我们得到了互联网这个大盘子，而互联网不一定以同样的速度增长——互联网上所有有用的东西都以同样的速度增长。所以我们可能还有一堆 0.1% 的损失下降可以拿，但肯定没有目前已经发生的那么多。

turns.en: But it's also really interesting that you find this—what, cumulative like 27 times improvement across both?
turns.zh: 但同样很有意思的是，你发现这个——总共累计大约 27 倍的提升，两者加起来？

ts.sec: Algorithmic Efficiency Gains and Scale Dependence

turns.en: I think it was Epoch or someone who estimated like three times a year since 2019, which would imply something like 3 to the 7, like over 2,000 times improvement. So where's that missing 100 times or whatever coming from? That probably gives you a good signal of how much of this is post-training.
turns.zh: 我记得是 Epoch 或者某个人估算过，自 2019 年以来大约每年提升三倍，那意味着 3 的 7 次方，也就是超过 2000 倍的提升。那缺失的那 100 倍左右是从哪来的？这大概能给你一个很好的信号，说明其中有多少来自后训练。

turns.en: I think the explanation has to be that a lot of the compute efficiency gains are scale dependent and we're studying at extremely small scale.
turns.zh: 我觉得解释只能是：很多算力效率的提升是依赖规模的，而我们是在极小的规模上做研究。

turns.en: And that raises the question of whether the data compute efficiency gains or the algorithmic compute efficiency gains have more scale dependence. I don't know if you guys have a prior on that. We just didn't have enough compute to investigate that question.
turns.zh: 这就引出一个问题：数据算力效率的提升，还是算法算力效率的提升，哪个更依赖规模？我不知道你们对此有没有先验判断。我们只是没有足够的算力去研究这个问题。

turns.en: I mean, just naively, right, theoretically the scale dependence of the architecture is fairly well-known, and you can fit a straight line to it. Whereas I would have no idea how to do that for combining pre-training plus post-training data and mid-training data.
turns.zh: 我是说，单纯从直觉上讲，理论上架构的规模依赖性是相当清楚的，你可以拟合出一条直线。但对于把预训练、后训练数据和中期训练数据结合起来，我完全不知道该怎么拟合。

turns.en: Funny enough, I feel like data is actually more important with scale. Like I feel like architectures are kind of a one-time thing, you know. I think combining, saying just an x% efficiency gain is kind of misleading, because what an architecture does is let you reach a qualitatively new regime which you couldn't reach with the old architecture. And then within that regime, obviously the data is the primary thing determining it. But if we didn't have even GQA, if we were doing full attention all day, we wouldn't be able to do a million context — it would be ridiculous expense to do a million context. And because of that, we could never use the data which is actually at a million context, and so we couldn't get these capabilities. Even though if you just do a naive 'how much does this do at 2k context' where the architecture isn't unlocking anything, then the data will look much more important than in some sense it is. It's unclear to me that these things are really just multiplicative gains in this way.
turns.zh: 说来有趣，我反而觉得数据在规模变大时更重要。我觉得架构有点像一次性的东西。我认为把效率提升简单说成“提升了 x%”是有点误导的，因为架构的作用是让你进入一个质变的新区间，这是旧架构到不了的。而在那个区间里，显然数据才是决定性的因素。但如果我们连 GQA 都没有，一直用全注意力，我们根本做不了百万上下文——做百万上下文的开销会高得离谱。正因为如此，我们就永远用不上那些真正处于百万上下文的数据，也就拿不到这些能力。可如果你只是天真地问“这东西在 2k 上下文下表现如何”，而架构在那里并没有解锁任何东西，那数据看起来就会比它实际上重要得多。我不确定这些东西真的只是这样相乘的增益。

turns.en: I see. So but then what is the takeaway for the scale dependence of data?
turns.zh: 我明白了。那么关于数据的规模依赖性，结论是什么？

turns.en: So on scale dependence, I think a lot of the mid-training and post-training data we have now actually gets better with scale, because a lot of it — the very long context horizon environments — really requires big models to be able to make use of them.
turns.zh: 关于规模依赖性，我觉得我们现在很多中期训练和后训练数据，其实是规模越大效果越好，因为其中很多——那些超长上下文视野的环境——确实需要大模型才能用得上。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: And this is not — you know, if you try and train your 100 million parameter model on three bench traces, it's not going to get anywhere. It's not going to show you the same kind of improvement that you would get if you train an actual sensible size model on it.
turns.zh: 而且这不是——你知道，如果你拿一个一亿参数的模型去训练三条 bench 轨迹，它根本不会有任何进展。它不会展现出你用真正合理规模的模型训练时能得到的那种提升。

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: Yeah. And it's hard as well now because so many of the architecture changes — you look at Kimi for instance, or DeepSeek — they're doing these architectural modifications not just with dropping the pre-training loss in mind, but for instance how the models are going to be used in the real world, the inference efficiency. Like having some form of compressed attention in the DeepSeek models is not necessarily geared around 'this is fundamentally an improvement' — it's just like, okay, we're considering how the models are going to be used.
turns.zh: 对。而且现在也很难，因为很多架构改动——你看 Kimi，或者 DeepSeek——他们做这些架构修改时，不只是想着降低预训练损失，还考虑比如模型在真实世界里会怎么被使用，也就是推理效率。比如 DeepSeek 模型里某种压缩注意力，未必是为了“这从根本上是个改进”，而只是说，好吧，我们在考虑模型会怎么被使用。

turns.en: Right, right. One question I'm curious about, to understand the future, is how parameter scaling will go as we're getting into more of an RL-heavy regime. I don't know how fast historically — you can look at open-source architectures and see how fast parameters have been scaling, and maybe it's roughly 2x every [year] for frontier open-source models. And to the extent that even frontier closed-source models have like 100b or 200b active parameters — do you think that keeps 2xing year over year? Or now that we're in an RL regime where you also want to conserve compute on rollouts, and also maybe there is a threshold effect where you have enough capacity and at that point increasing parameters arbitrarily doesn't matter as much. Do you guys have a sense of in 2030 how many active parameters will a frontier model have?
turns.zh: 对，对。我很好奇的一个问题，为了理解未来，是在我们越来越进入强化学习为主的范式时，参数规模会怎么走。我不知道历史上有多快——你可以看开源架构，看参数增长得多快，前沿开源模型大概是每年翻一倍。而即便前沿闭源模型也只有 1000 亿或 2000 亿激活参数——你觉得这还会逐年翻倍吗？还是说现在我们处在强化学习范式里，你还要在 rollout 上节省算力，而且也许存在阈值效应，容量够了之后，再随意增加参数就没那么重要了。你们觉得到 2030 年，一个前沿模型会有多少激活参数？

turns.en: Yeah, I think for the next few years, because we're so focused on doing longer and longer horizon rollouts for RL, where inference efficiency matters a lot — it feels like the models aren't necessarily saturated on their ability to do that, where the bottleneck is still the environments. And so we might see a little bit of plateau. I have a feeling that, you know, like Mythos and the GPT models are much smaller than the 10 trillion parameter range that people are talking about. Even just naively comparing them to open-source models, you can probably back out that conclusion.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得未来几年，因为我们非常专注于为强化学习做越来越长视野的 rollout，而推理效率在那里很重要——感觉模型在这方面的能力还没饱和，瓶颈仍然在环境上。所以我们可能会看到一点平台期。我有种感觉，像 Mythos 和 GPT 系列模型，比人们谈论的 10 万亿参数规模要小得多。就算只是天真地和开源模型对比一下，你大概也能反推出这个结论。

turns.en: So yeah, probably for the next few years I wouldn't imagine a huge growth in the number of parameters. But again, there are so many different things to trade off here. You decide the size of your model based on how much pre-training data you have, and then the difficulty of the RL environments that you've got to train on. And you ideally want to get to the optimal point where you can get a decent pass at one or something on the hardest environments you have, and it wouldn't make sense to make a bigger model pass there because then you're just paying much more inference flops than you need to. So there's a lot of input to this — it depends on how quickly, you know, like Mccor and then in-house these guys can scale up the complexity of the rollout environments they're training on.
turns.zh: 所以是的，未来几年我大概不会预期参数数量有巨大增长。但话说回来，这里要权衡的东西太多了。你根据自己有多少预训练数据，以及要训练的强化学习环境的难度，来决定模型大小。理想情况下你想达到最优点：在你最难的环境上能拿到不错的通过率之类的，而把模型做得更大去通过那里就没意义了，因为那样你只是在付远超所需的推理算力。所以这有很多输入因素——取决于像 Mccor 以及内部这些团队能多快把训练用的 rollout 环境的复杂度扩上去。

turns.en: I would expect the models to keep getting bigger, just because people are scaling up compute and the GPUs are getting bigger. But I would say exactly how much they get bigger depends a bit on the scaling laws in non-obvious ways. So one thing is that I think data efficiency is going to be a bigger driver than compute efficiency of the exact architectures people use, now that we're getting to the regime where we're sort of running low on high quality pre-training data. So that might affect how sparse you want to make the model. And then I also think we don't understand sparsity that well.
turns.zh: 我预期模型会继续变大，因为人们在扩大算力，GPU 也越来越大。但具体变大多少，会以不那么显然的方式取决于缩放定律。一点是，我觉得在人们实际采用的架构上，数据效率会比算力效率成为更大的驱动因素，因为我们现在正进入高质量预训练数据有点快用完的范式。这可能会影响你想把模型做得多稀疏。另外我也觉得我们对稀疏性的理解还不够好。

turns.en: And it's like parameters are a different resource than active parameters, but sparsity has definitely increased a bit, but it's not clear that it's going to keep increasing without bound. There might be some kind of sweet spot.
turns.zh: 而且参数和激活参数是不同的资源，但稀疏性确实增加了一些，不过不清楚它会不会无限制地一直增加。可能存在某种最佳平衡点。

turns.en: There's an argument that sparsity should make data efficiency worse, because you might have to learn the same thing on multiple experts.
turns.zh: 有一种观点认为，稀疏性会让数据效率变差，因为你可能得在多个专家上学习同样的东西。

turns.en: Though that's debatable. I think we don't — I don't think we have a good enough theory of scaling laws that we really understand why sparsity is helping, to what extent it'll help, and whether it'll plateau at some point at a certain level of sparsity.
turns.zh: 不过这还有争议。我觉得我们对缩放定律的理论还不够完善，没法真正理解稀疏性为什么有用、能有多大帮助，以及它是否会在某个稀疏程度上遇到瓶颈。

turns.en: Sorry, can you spell out exactly what the implication of data efficiency would be? So it sounds like you'd say there should be less sparsity, but what are the other implications on parameter scaling?
turns.zh: 抱歉，你能具体说明一下数据效率会带来什么影响吗？听起来你会说稀疏度应该更低，但它对参数规模还有什么其他影响？

turns.en: I guess just that in the scaling law you're not necessarily looking for the most — you're not trying to optimize compute efficiency. So you have all your choices you can make on the architecture, and each of these gives you a different scaling law, and then traditionally you would look at some kind of envelope based on compute. So you would look at performance versus compute and take the envelope of the best models. But if we're making that decision based on data, so it's like we're sort of assuming we can spend a lot of compute, and we're sort of putting data on our x-axis instead of compute, then we just get a different set of optima or a different set of models that are on that frontier.
turns.zh: 我想只是说，在缩放定律里你不一定追求最高的——你不是在优化算力效率。你在架构上有一堆可选的设计，每一种都给出不同的缩放定律，传统上你会看某种基于算力的包络线。也就是看性能对算力的关系，取最好模型的包络。但如果我们基于数据来做这个决策，也就是假设我们可以花很多算力，把数据放在 x 轴上而不是算力，那我们就会得到一组不同的最优点，或者前沿上一组不同的模型。

turns.en: Yeah. And I also don't think that we've necessarily doubled the size of the models every year for the last few years. People have been training one-trillion-parameter models for at least a few years. There was even an open source one called Falcon. But Liam from Periodic Labs posted yesterday on Twitter about how an early experiment at OpenAI was training a one-trillion-parameter model that was very, very sparse.
turns.zh: 对。而且我也不认为过去几年我们每年都把模型规模翻了一倍。人们训练万亿参数模型至少已经有好几年了，甚至还有一个开源的叫 Falcon。但 Periodic Labs 的 Liam 昨天在 Twitter 上发帖说，OpenAI 早期有个实验训练了一个非常非常稀疏的万亿参数模型。

turns.en: Oh yeah. That was what they did before OpenAI — that was like at Google, the switch. Yeah. So it was very, very good at knowledge but terrible at reasoning because it was so sparse. And so it feels like we've been playing in this 100 billion up to two trillion parameter range for at least a little bit, and it certainly hasn't been this nice linear increase.
turns.zh: 哦对。那是 OpenAI 之前做的——那是在 Google，那个 switch。对。所以它在知识上非常非常强，但推理很糟糕，因为太稀疏了。所以感觉我们至少在 1000 亿到 2 万亿参数这个区间里玩了一阵子了，而且肯定不是那种漂亮的线性增长。

turns.en: Yeah, I mean I feel like there's two things. As Charlie was saying, inference efficiency is super important for RL rollouts, and so this will really push down active parameters quite a lot. And then I think the total parameters really depends a lot on the hardware as well. You really need to get very high memory bandwidth and VRAM size to actually be able to serve multi-trillion parameter models. Right now people are still using a lot of H100s and stuff, and so as everyone moves to GBs and then Vera Rubins, we'll get more of the ability to scale and actually serve and do large RL inputs at larger scales.
turns.zh: 对，我觉得有两件事。就像 Charlie 说的，推理效率对强化学习的 rollout 超级重要，所以这会大幅压低活跃参数量。然后我觉得总参数量很大程度上也取决于硬件。你确实需要非常高的内存带宽和显存容量，才能真正服务多参数万亿级的模型。现在大家还在用很多 H100 之类的东西，所以随着大家转向 GB 系列、再到 Vera Rubin，我们会有更强的能力去扩展、去实际服务，并在更大规模上做大型强化学习输入。

turns.en: The data crunch I think is interesting because naively larger models are much more sample efficient in terms of actual data points, and so even if you're not saturating the model, it's still better to go bigger because larger models generalize better and get to a better loss for the same amount of data. And so right now I think we kind of have a lot of data and that's not the constraint rather than compute, and so we're having small models which are very inference efficient. But if compute's no longer the bottleneck, it might come back to larger models which are sort of undersaturated but have this generalization ability because they're larger.
turns.zh: 数据瓶颈我觉得很有意思，因为直觉上更大的模型在实际数据点上的样本效率高得多，所以即使你没有把模型训练到饱和，做大仍然更好，因为更大的模型泛化更好，在同样的数据量下能达到更低的损失。所以现在我觉得我们数据还挺多，瓶颈不是数据而是算力，于是我们做小模型，推理效率很高。但如果算力不再是瓶颈，可能又会回到更大的模型，它们有点欠饱和，但因为更大而有这种泛化能力。

turns.en: If you just look at the basic Chinchilla scaling law and you just maximize out parameters —
turns.zh: 如果你只看基本的 Chinchilla 缩放定律，把参数最大化——

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: — it actually decreases the amount of data you need to get to the same loss very little.
turns.zh: ——它其实只会让你达到同样损失所需的数据量减少一点点。

turns.en: Yes. If you go to infinity on parameters, the amount of data you need, I think, goes down less than 10x, just because of the nature of the power law.
turns.zh: 对。如果参数趋于无穷，我觉得所需数据量下降不到 10 倍，就是因为幂律的性质。

turns.en: We're now on the way-too-much-data side of the Chinchilla laws, right? So right now we overtrain models according to Chinchilla, and so we could easily go back to a point where, as we're running out of data, we move back to the Chinchilla optimal point or even a bit on the overtraining — you know, undertraining model side. But surely even with these new chips that come online and stuff, we're just going to be so compute bottlenecked for the next few years that that won't necessarily—
turns.zh: 我们现在处在 Chinchilla 定律里数据太多的那一侧，对吧？现在我们是按 Chinchilla 过度训练模型，所以很容易回到一个点：随着数据耗尽，我们回到 Chinchilla 最优点，甚至稍微偏向过度训练——也就是模型训练不足的那一侧。但肯定的是，即使有这些新芯片上线，未来几年我们还是会严重受限于算力，那就不一定——

turns.en: I mean, this could well — yeah, this depends on the ratio you have with training and inference compute really. If you're super bottlenecked on data, not on compute, you should go bigger. If you're super bottlenecked on compute, you should always go smaller. But you can also use compute to generate synthetic data. So it's one of these very hard things to predict.
turns.zh: 这很可能——对，这真的取决于训练算力和推理算力的比例。如果你严重受限于数据而不是算力，就该做大。如果你严重受限于算力，就总该做小。但你也可以用算力生成合成数据。所以这是很难预测的事情之一。

turns.en: Yeah. I think part of the reason it took people so long to figure out the scaling laws in the first place was that if you don't get all these things right, then you don't get such a clean relationship. And the beautiful straight lines on graphs hide a lot of complexity in how you have to make sure to scale every hyperparameter the right way, or parameterize your optimizer in a way that scales and where you don't have to change your hyperparameters as you change the model size.
turns.zh: 对。我觉得人们一开始花了那么久才搞清缩放定律，部分原因是如果你没把这些都做对，就得不到这么干净的关系。图上那些漂亮的直线掩盖了很多复杂性：你得确保每个超参数都按正确方式缩放，或者把优化器参数化得能扩展，并且改变模型规模时不用改超参数。

turns.en: And bugs have their own clean scaling laws as well, right? Like with Kaplan forgetting the cosine thing, or even just not considering embedding parameters — I think that messed up the estimate at smaller models because embedding parameters are a decent size of the model.
turns.zh: 而且 bug 也有它们自己干净的缩放定律，对吧？比如 Kaplan 忘了余弦那件事，甚至只是没考虑嵌入参数——我觉得那搞乱了小模型上的估计，因为嵌入参数在模型里占比不小。

ts.sec: Why RL scaled better than expected

turns.en: A bit on RL. I feel like a year ago a lot of people were making this argument that RL will not be super successful at scaling for models. I think, John, you wrote a research paper where you were pointing out that models learn one bit per episode when you RL — basically learn did I get the answer right or did I get it wrong. And I wrote some blog post earlier this year saying it's even worse than that, because when the pass rate is low, when the model is very unlikely to get the answer right, it learns almost nothing at all from an RL episode. But I look at the models today and they seem pretty smart, and it seems to be the result of scaling up RL. Beren, you had a post a few weeks ago where you were trying to explain what's going on. But why has RL been more successful than one would have naively thought?
turns.zh: 聊一点强化学习。我感觉一年前很多人都在说，强化学习在模型扩展上不会特别成功。John，我记得你写过一篇研究论文，指出模型在强化学习时每个回合只学一个比特——基本上就是学“我答对了还是答错了”。我今年早些时候写过一篇博客说，情况比那还糟，因为当通过率很低、模型几乎不可能答对时，它从一个强化学习回合里几乎什么都学不到。但我看今天的模型，它们似乎挺聪明的，而且似乎是扩大强化学习规模的结果。Beren，你几周前发过一个帖子试图解释这是怎么回事。但为什么强化学习比人们直觉上以为的更成功？

turns.en: I mean, I think the success of RL comes down to a bunch of different things. First, I think what is slightly underestimated is actually the mid-training.
turns.zh: 我觉得强化学习的成功归结于好几个不同的因素。首先，我觉得被稍微低估的其实是中期训练。

turns.en: So an awful lot of what we see as successes of RL actually comes from very, very good mid-training data, which is basically where we're essentially doing pre-training but on synthetic reasoning data and the kind of environments that get the model warm-started for RL. And so this actually takes the model almost 80% of the way to the final RL checkpoint often. And then what RL does on top of that is essentially a lot of tweaking to the policy. And so this is one of the reasons why it doesn't need as many bits as you would naively think. It doesn't have to learn all of these behaviors from scratch. It needs just a few bits from these episodes, which you do get. And then the other thing that I really point out in my blog is that these bits are actually extremely high signal compared to regular pre-training, which is why you need RL at all versus just SFTing on successful reasoning traces.
turns.zh: 我们看到的大量 RL 成功案例，其实来自非常好的中训练数据——基本上就是我们在做预训练，只不过用的是合成推理数据，以及那些能让模型为 RL 热启动的环境。所以这往往能把模型带到距离最终 RL 检查点大约 80% 的位置。然后 RL 在上面做的，本质上是对策略做大量微调。这也是为什么它不需要你天真以为的那么多比特。它不必从零学会所有这些行为，只需要从这些回合里拿到几个比特，而这些你确实能拿到。然后我在博客里特别指出的另一点是：相比常规预训练，这些比特的信号强度极高，这正是为什么你需要 RL，而不是只对成功的推理轨迹做 SFT。

turns.en: Well, there's two things. So yes, one, it's exactly the bits about how to get the answer right. But this is not exactly how you think of it, because in SFT you have a trace, right? You have a bunch of math reasoning and then the answer at the end. The bit is still there. You still SFT on the answer token. So that bit is still there. What's important is that the objective ignores all the other bits. So in SFT you have to try and match the exact reasoning tokens that the model produces. So you're essentially getting too many bits about the exact way this other model you're training on reasons. For RL you only get the one bit, and that means that signal is not drowned out in the noise of all the other bits the model has. And so that's what really dramatically increases the signal-to-noise ratio during training, which is why RL is so dramatically efficient in terms of steps. I don't know if you guys have thoughts on that.
turns.zh: 嗯，有两点。是的，第一，它确实就是关于如何得到正确答案的那些比特。但事情并不完全像你想的那样，因为在 SFT 里你有一条轨迹，对吧？你有一堆数学推理，然后最后是答案。那个比特仍然在。你仍然对答案 token 做 SFT。所以那个比特仍然在。重要的是，目标函数忽略了所有其他比特。在 SFT 里，你得努力去匹配模型产生的那些确切的推理 token。所以你实际上拿到了太多关于你正在训练的这个模型具体如何推理的比特。而在 RL 里你只拿到那一个比特，这意味着那个信号不会被模型所有其他比特的噪声淹没。所以这才是真正在训练中大幅提高信噪比的东西，也是为什么 RL 在步数上效率如此之高。不知道你们对此有什么想法。

turns.en: Yeah, there's been so much debate about what RL does to the model versus mid-training or SFT or whatever. And everyone talks about how pass@1 will go up but pass@256 will go down, that very rare correct reasoning traces will be down-weighted and kind of outweighed by gradient signal from easier reasoning traces. And I think the simple way to view RL now is that if you have a large enough amount of compute to sample a large enough group size such that your probability of getting a bunch of correct answers is past some not insignificant probability, then it will be upweighted. And to Von's point, basically mid-training and more pre-training—the pass@1, the starting point for RL—scales in a log number of pre-training tokens.
turns.zh: 是啊，关于 RL 对模型做了什么、相比中训练或 SFT 之类的，争论一直很多。大家都在说 pass@1 会上升，但 pass@256 会下降，那些非常罕见的正确推理轨迹会被降权，会被来自更容易的推理轨迹的梯度信号压过去。我觉得现在看 RL 的一个简单方式是：如果你有足够大的算力去采样足够大的组大小，使得你得到一堆正确答案的概率超过某个不算微不足道的概率，那它就会被升权。而且就像 Von 说的，基本上中训练和更多预训练——也就是 RL 的起点 pass@1——是随预训练 token 数的对数增长的。

ts.sec: Squaring small bit impact with capability gains

turns.en: You can ask some very basic questions. I guess that answer makes sense, and maybe there's empirical research which shows that this is what's happening. But then I just look at the models themselves and I don't know what's happened. Maybe you can give me a sense of what is the basis of the AI progress over the last year. But if it's—maybe it's just upweighting the policies which were going to do the correct thinking anyways—but it just seems like qualitatively the models have gotten so much more capable. And maybe there's no inherent contradiction there, but how do we square the relatively small impact this take would imply that RL would have with the actual qualitative capabilities the models seem to be gaining?
turns.zh: 你可以问一些非常基础的问题。我想那个回答说得通，也许有实证研究表明事情就是这样。但然后我就看看模型本身，我不知道发生了什么。也许你可以给我讲讲过去一年 AI 进步的根基是什么。但如果它——也许它只是给那些本来就会做正确思考的策略升权——但看起来在质上模型变得强太多了。也许那里并没有内在矛盾，但我们怎么把这个观点所暗示的 RL 影响相对较小，与模型似乎正在获得的实际质性能力对上呢？

turns.en: So one thing I want to point out here is that it doesn't necessarily imply that RL has a small effect, right? Even if you have a few bits and you only change the parameters a small amount, the actual impact on the function space of the model—the input-output mapping—can still be super dramatic. Even one bit can change your function space a lot, and it can rule out half the hypothesis space, which is huge. So I don't think it's necessarily the case that small amounts of bits, small amounts of RL once you're starting from a really good point, means you don't have dramatic impacts in behavior—at least not necessarily.
turns.zh: 这里我想指出的一点是，它并不必然意味着 RL 的影响小，对吧？即使你只有几个比特，只对参数做了很小的改动，对模型函数空间——也就是输入输出映射——的实际影响仍然可能非常巨大。哪怕一个比特也能大幅改变你的函数空间，它能排除掉一半的假设空间，这非常大。所以我不认为从很好的起点出发、少量比特、少量 RL，就必然意味着行为上没有巨大影响——至少不一定。

turns.en: I think it comes down to two things. Because I think the first thing is that everyone was hoping that RL would generalize this reasoning across all these different domains, and I don't think we necessarily got this horizontal generalization—just training on math doesn't necessarily make you the greatest coder, you do have to do RL on code environments. I think what we did get though is horizon generalization. The models just learned how to use more tokens for longer and still make progress on some sort of task. And so you can train on environments where they get longer and longer and longer, and then put them into a completely new environment, and yes, they may not have generalized the reasoning patterns which allow them to do well in that environment, but they've at least generalized the ability to continue on that task for longer, which is correlated with success. I think there's a paper called EdgeBench which showed that the rate at which models can work for longer is doubling every 3 months. And so that's clear evidence of generalization. And I think the final way to think about it is: in pre-training there's this idea of quanta. So you have this very smooth pre-training loss curve. And when you actually look at what's happening in the model, the model is learning all these very discrete tasks, and there are all these emergent points where there's kind of a phase transition—it didn't have induction heads, now it has induction heads—and there are tens of thousands, millions, probably hundreds of millions of these things, and you average them all together and you get this very smooth loss curve. I think to an extent a similar thing is happening for RL. There is this very slow ad loop, as Beren mentioned, of we will train a model and then RL it, and then the next model iteration of training we will dump a bunch of these synthetic reasoning traces into the mid-training data. We're kind of hitting all these quanta for all these different tasks, and on an individual task level it may look like a phase transition, like you're suddenly going from a 5% pass rate to a 90% pass rate on a particular finance task or Excel task.
turns.zh: 我觉得这归结为两点。因为我认为第一点是，大家都希望 RL 能把这种推理泛化到所有这些不同领域，而我不认为我们必然得到了这种横向泛化——只在数学上训练并不一定让你成为最厉害的编程者，你确实得在代码环境上做 RL。不过我认为我们确实得到的是视野泛化。模型就是学会了如何用更多 token 工作更久，并且仍然在某种任务上取得进展。所以你可以让它们在越来越长的环境上训练，然后把它们放进一个全新的环境，是的，它们可能没有泛化出能让它们在那个环境里表现好的推理模式，但它们至少泛化了继续做那个任务更久的能力，而这与成功相关。我记得有一篇叫 EdgeBench 的论文，它表明模型能工作更久的能力大约每 3 个月翻一倍。所以这是泛化的明确证据。我觉得最后一种理解方式是：预训练里有量子（quanta）这个概念。你有一条非常平滑的预训练损失曲线。而当你真正看模型内部发生了什么，模型在学所有这些非常离散的任务，有所有这些涌现点，那里有点像相变——它之前没有归纳头，现在有了归纳头——这样的东西有成千上万、数百万，可能上亿个，你把它们平均在一起，就得到这条非常平滑的损失曲线。我觉得在某种程度上，RL 也在发生类似的事。正如 Beren 提到的，有一个非常缓慢的循环：我们训练一个模型，然后对它做 RL，然后在下一个模型迭代的训练中，我们会把一堆这样的合成推理轨迹倒进中训练数据里。我们有点像在为所有这些不同任务命中所有这些量子，而在单个任务层面，它可能看起来像相变，比如你在某个特定的金融任务或 Excel 任务上突然从 5% 的通过率跳到 90% 的通过率。

turns.en: Ask or whatever, but you average all these things together and plus the horizon generalization, you kind of will go, wow, we've got like qualitatively better models.
turns.zh: 随便问吧，但你把所有这些平均起来，再加上横向泛化，你会觉得，哇，我们有了质的提升的模型。

turns.en: Yeah. I mean, I think a lot of this as well is just like I think RL does generalize a bit like suddenly you get like some transfer between like math and code or like puzzles and math and this kind of stuff. Also just like the amount the sheer amount of environments I think the people are targeting is just like vastly greater. So like you know before when you try to do you know some task which like you do in your daily life like two years ago like the labs wouldn't really care about this. they wouldn't like train the model for it and now like it's just so much broader. They have a lot of environments targeting this specific thing.
turns.zh: 是的。我觉得很多也在于，我认为强化学习确实有一点泛化，比如突然之间数学和代码之间、谜题和数学之间会有一些迁移。另外，人们针对的环境数量也大大增加了。所以你知道，以前你尝试做日常生活中的某个任务，两年前实验室根本不会关心这个，他们不会为此训练模型，而现在范围广多了。他们有很多针对这个特定事物的环境。

turns.en: Early in the conversation we're talking about are all in the context of causing this entropy collapse or just you know concentrating probability on solutions the base model were already done. Um and causing relatively sparse updates in the policy. Um, but when I think like when I think about I think the there's also another story about RL which is going back to the Atari games and then AlphaGo coming up with move 37, the super creative move that because it was never initialized on human data, it can like think in ways that humans are not even thinking and come up with extremely creative solutions.
turns.zh: 在对话早期，我们讨论的都是导致这种熵坍缩的语境，或者只是把概率集中在基础模型已经完成的解决方案上，以及导致策略中相对稀疏的更新。但是当我想到强化学习时，我认为还有另一个故事，那就是回到 Atari 游戏，然后 AlphaGo 下出第 37 手，那个超级有创造性的 move，因为它从未在人类数据上初始化，所以它可以以人类甚至没有想到的方式思考，并提出极具创造性的解决方案。

turns.en: Yeah. Do you have a sense on when we should expect or if we should expect RL on LLMs to result in things like move 37 just extreme creativity even beyond human creativity because like there's just denovo uh dova initialization of intelligence.

consensus.en: The last human job is defining objectives and alignment; AI can do technical work but not decide what we want.
consensus.zh: 人类最后的工作是定义目标与对齐；AI 能完成技术工作，却无法决定我们真正想要什么。

consensus.en: RL's success stems largely from mid-training synthetic reasoning data plus high signal-to-noise from one-bit rewards.
consensus.zh: 强化学习的成功主要来自后训练前的合成推理数据，以及单比特奖励带来的高信噪比。

consensus.en: Distillation fights centralization because RL-learned behaviors are few bits and easily copied.
consensus.zh: 蒸馏对抗中心化，因为强化学习学到的行为比特少、极易被复制。

consensus.en: Sim-to-real remains dominant while sample efficiency is low; deployment learning will grow as efficiency improves.
consensus.zh: 样本效率低时模拟到现实仍是主流；效率提升后从部署中学习会增多。

consensus.en: Horizon generalization, not horizontal reasoning transfer, is what RL reliably delivers across domains.
consensus.zh: 强化学习可靠带来的是时间跨度泛化，而非跨领域的横向推理迁移。

consensus.en: Progress is bottlenecked less by compute than by creating hard, realistic RL environments and useful data bits.
consensus.zh: 进展瓶颈不在算力，而在构建困难、真实的强化学习环境和有用的数据比特。

contrarian.en: Next-token prediction on naive log loss was expected to fail, yet it generalized far beyond any reasonable expectation.
contrarian.zh: 朴素对数损失上的下一个词预测本被认为会失败，却泛化得远超任何合理预期。

contrarian.en: RL does not destroy creativity; models already show move-37-like zero-day creativity from general generalization.
contrarian.zh: 强化学习并未摧毁创造力；模型已凭泛化展现出类似第37手的零日创造力。

contrarian.en: Small RL bit counts can dramatically reshape function space; few bits do not mean small behavioral impact.
contrarian.zh: 少量强化学习比特也能剧烈重塑函数空间；比特少不代表行为影响小。

contrarian.en: Data, not architecture, explains most pre-training compute-efficiency gains, roughly 9x versus 3x.
contrarian.zh: 预训练算力效率提升主要来自数据而非架构，约9倍对3倍。

contrarian.en: Parameter counts may plateau as inference efficiency for long-horizon RL rollouts dominates model sizing.
contrarian.zh: 随着长跨度强化学习推演看重推理效率，参数规模可能趋于平台期。

contrarian.en: RSI may be a cumulative task easier than messy real-world work like being a legal associate.
contrarian.zh: 递归自我改进或许是累积型任务，比当法务助理这类混乱现实工作更简单。
